(a) Flow chart of patient dataset and analyses (top panels). Venn diagrams summarizing the number of patients with quantified architecture in the tumour-core (CT) and invasive-margin (IM) compartments (bottom panel). (b) Number of analysed TMA cores per patient for each compartment (tumour core and invasive margin). (c) Representative images of tumour cores and invasive margins. Yellow dashed lines indicate the tumour–stroma boundary. Scale bar 200 µm. (d) Kaplan-Meier survival curves for patients stratified by nuclear circularity (high, medium, low) of tumour core (left) or invasive margin (right). P-values pairwise log-rank test. (e, f) Multivariate Cox proportional hazards models including the circularity shape descriptor, comparing stage II–III (e) or stage I (f) patients (p-values Wald). (g) Average nuclear shapes (area, circularity, and solidity) per patient, across tumour stages (patient-level permutation tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction). Half-violins show the kernel density estimate of the distribution of per-patient values. Boxplots show median, 25th–75th percentile (IQR), and 1.5×IQR whiskers. (h) Representative images of the six tumour architecture archetypes (scale bar 200 µm; architecture was quantified in 1,037 patients (a)).

(a) Representative invasive margin sample with heterogeneous architectures (left panel), classifier predictions, projection of three closest neighbours’ distances, and relative alignment (order). Scale bar 400 µm. (b) t-SNE embedding of features derived from the U-Net from tiles used for classifier training. (c) Precision and recall of the tile classifier for architecture classification across classes, with error bars representing the standard deviation from five-fold cross-validation. (d) Schematic representation of quantified histological features, including neighbourhood, morphological and tumour-stroma interactions features. (e) Silhouette scores of the 196 manually selected archetype cores in morphological feature space (12 features from Fig. 1f: neighbourhood, stroma, morphology), compared to size-matched random draws from the MSS cohort with matching per-class label counts (n = 1,000 permutations). Distribution of mean silhouette scores across random draws (grey histogram) with the archetype value (black dashed line; left panel). Per-class silhouette (right panel): violins show the null distribution; diamonds mark the archetype silhouette for each architectural subtype. Archetypes form tighter, better-separated clusters than random draws overall and within each class, indicating that the manual curation captured genuine, well-defined exemplars of each architectural subtype rather than arbitrary selections.

(a) Multivariate Cox proportional hazards models incorporating architecture types, with Glandular as the reference. Fragmented architecture remains significantly associated with poor survival after adjustment for other covariates. Estimated log hazard ratio (Cox regression coefficient) with 95% CI are shown; dashed vertical line at log(HR) = 0 indicates no effect (Wald tests with robust standard errors; p-values not adjusted for multiple comparisons). (b) Stacked bar plot displaying the distribution of architecture types across tumour stages, with left bars representing the tumour core and right bars representing the invasive margin. (c) Kaplan-Meier survival curves for stage II–III patients, stratified by architecture type from tumour core (CT) and invasive margin (IM). Patients with fragmented architectures exhibit poorer survival. (d) Kaplan-Meier survival curves for stage I–IV MSI patients, stratified by architecture type. (e, f) Kaplan-Meier survival curves of the validation dataset for MSS patients at stage I–IV (left) and stage II–III (right) (e) and for MSI patients at stage I–IV (f), stratified by architecture type. Validation dataset recapitulates poor survival in fragmented architecture MSS patients. (g) Sankey diagram illustrating the correspondence between CT and IM architecture classifications. (h) Distribution of the fragmentation index per TMA core, comparing values between the tumour core and invasive margin (paired sign-flip permutation test on log1p-transformed patient-level compartment means; n = 518 paired patients; boxplots show median IQR; 1.5×IQR whiskers). For all Kaplan-Meier curves p-values were from pairwise log-rank tests versus Glandular reference group.

(a) Stacked bar plot of budding grade distribution across architectures in tumour cores (CT). (b) Kaplan-Meier curves with low budding (BD1) grade, stratified by tumour architecture. (c) Distribution of intratumoral budding in CT classified as fragmented (left) or between mildly and strongly fragmented (right). (d, e) Normalized distribution of histological subtypes (d) and tumour grade (e; Low: grade 1–2; High: grade 3–4) across architecture types. Patients with unknown grade excluded. (f) Kaplan-Meier curves stratified by tumour architecture in CT (high-grade, left; low-grade, right; stages II–III; MSS; age <85). (g) Heatmap showing percentage of patients classified as fragmented within grade and tumour budding category (BD1: 0-4 buds; BD2: 5-9 buds; BD3: ≥10 buds; MSS; CT; age <85). (h) Hazard ratios (log scale) for disease-specific survival in stage II–III MSS (age <85). Patients with unknown budding or grade excluded. Analysis performed separately for CT (green) and IM (pink). Estimated log hazard ratio (Cox regression coefficient) with 95% CI; dashed vertical line at log(HR) = 0 indicates no effect, Wald tests with robust standard errors; p-values not adjusted for multiple comparisons). (i, j) Distribution of tumour location (i) and Immunoscore (j) across architecture classifications in MSS. Proportions normalized per architecture group. (k) Half-violin plots with embedded box plots showing per-core mean nuclear circularity (left) and solidity (right) for IM. Only IM cores with a dominant architecture (mixed cores excluded) and nuclear morphometry data were included; n is therefore lower than in Fig. 1h (871 IM patients). Each dot represents one TMA core; values are mean of all tumour nuclei within that core (n = 728 cores from 571 patients: Gland, n = 455 cores/372 patients; Sol, n = 24 cores/22 patients; Frag, n = 249 cores/206 patients; patient-level permutation tests on per-patient architecture means with Benjamini-Hochberg; boxplots show median, IQR; 1.5×IQR whiskers). For all Kaplan-Meier curves p-values were from pairwise log-rank tests versus Glandular group.

(a) Number of transcriptomic regions per patient, stratified by compartment (tumour core vs. invasive margin) and tissue type (tumour on left, stroma on right). (b) Distribution of molecular clusters across patients, demonstrating that each patient harbours unique clusters. (c) Distribution of architectural patterns among transcriptomic regions in each patient; most patients display heterogeneous architectures. (d) Distribution of molecular clusters across spatial clusters (excluding patients with few regions), where each spatial cluster is transcriptionally homogeneous. (e) Distribution of architecture types across spatial clusters (excluding patients with few regions), with each cluster exhibiting consistent architectural profiles. (f) Spatial projections of tumour slides for patients 6 (top) and 3 (bottom), with colour coding for architectures (left) and molecular clusters (right). Scale bar 5 mm. (g–i) Heatmaps showing the top 50 differentially expressed genes across architecture types for crypt base (g), regenerative stem cell (h), and EMT (i) gene sets.

(a) Heatmap of key cell state and morphological marker levels in indicated cellular compartments across Leiden phenotypic cell macroclusters (cyto = cytoplasmic; nuc = nuclear). Grey bars indicate cell number in each cluster. Diff = differentiated, Reg = regenerative. (b) Bar graph of distribution of cell macroclusters to generate patient-scale phenotypic groups. Grey bars indicate the number of patients in each group. (c) Representative immunofluorescence images (out of 1037 patients) of ANXA1, TNC, CDX2, pan-cytokeratin (panCK), and Ki67 stainings of patient TMAs in the main phenotypic groups to identify relationships of cell phenotypes with tumour architecture. Numbers indicate the corresponding zoomed regions (white rectangles in upper panel). Colours indicate the corresponding molecular clusters. Scale bars 200 µm (upper panel), 100 µm (lower panel).

(a) Representative images of TMA cores illustrating four architecture-epithelial state combinations (1: Gland-Reg/EMT; 2: Gland-Prox1; 3: Frag-Proliferative; 4: Frag-Diff). Top row: composite immunofluorescence overlay (DAPI, ANXA1, PROX1, CDX2, panCK, Ki67). Middle rows: individual channel images for each marker (DAPI, ANXA1, TNC, PROX1, VIM, CDX2, panCK, Ki67, E-Cadherin). Bottom row: cell-level epithelial state classification maps with per-cell colour coding (PROX1, (Diff-Low, Diff-High, Diff-Mid, Proliferative, Reg/EMT, EMT VIM; scale bars 200 µm; 100 µm)). (b) Kaplan-Meier curve of disease-specific survival across architecture and tumour phenotypic composite groups in invasive margin (IM; pairwise log-rank tests versus the Gland-Diff High reference group). (c) Kaplan-Meier curves for disease-specific survival in stage II-III patients, stratified by combined architecture–epithelial state categories in tumour core (CT; top) and IM (bottom). Fragmented-Regen/EMT tumours show the worst prognosis in the CT (pairwise log-rank tests versus the Gland-Diff-High reference group). (d) Kaplan-Meier curves for disease-specific survival stratified by dominant tumour epithelial state in the core tumour (CT, top) and invasive margin (IM, bottom). No significant survival differences were observed between epithelial states in the CT. In contrast, Diff-Low and Regen/EMT states associate with worse prognosis in the IM (pairwise log-rank tests versus the Diff-High reference group). (e) Sankey diagram plot showing the redistribution of architecture–epithelial state combinations between CT and IM compartments. Most patients with fragmented regenerative tumour cores also showed the same signature at the invasive margin, whereas the reverse pattern was less frequent. Gland = glandular, Frag = fragmented, Reg = regenerative, Diff = differentiated.

(a) UMAP projection of Leiden clusters from single cell RNAseq data of CRC patients from Pelka et al. (b) Gene set enrichment analyses of CBC, Regenerative stem cell (SC) and EMT states from (a), note co-enrichment of Regenerative SC and EMT states in cluster 3. (c) UMAP projection of Leiden clusters from single cell RNAseq data of CRC patients from Lee et al. (d) Gene set enrichment analyses of CBC, Regenerative SC and EMT states from (c), note co-enrichment of Regenerative SC and EMT states in cluster 3. (e, f) Dotplots (e) and Pearson’s correlation heatmaps (f) of single cells from selected Leiden clusters (e) or across entire dataset (f) scored using CBC, Regenerative SC and EMT gene sets. Note positive correlation of Regenerative SC and EMT signatures and anticorrelation of CBC signatures in single cells. (g) Correlation dotplots of individual key identity markers in single cells from Pelka Leiden cluster 3. (h, i) CytoTRACE scoring for stemness (h) and diffusion pseudotime (i) analyses of CBC to EMT/Regenerative SC states from Pelka subclustered cells (clusters 0,3,4,6 in full dataset). (j) Key transcription factor and identity marker expression across pseudotime. Cells were binned into 50 pseudotime bins per trajectory, expression values were averaged in each bin and z-transformed across both trajectories.

(a) Quantification of SNAIL1, VIM, and nuclear/cytoplasmic ANXA1 immunofluorescence across three tumour architectures, derived from multiple regions of two whole-slide sections from two patients (two-sided Mann-Whitney/Benjamini-Hochberg (BH)). (b) Projected mean intensity of nuclear and cytoplasmic ANXA1 in individual tumour cells at the invasive front of Patient 8 exhibiting moderate fragmentation (top panels), corresponding box-and-violin plots (lower panel) show ANXA1 intensity across distance bins relative to the invasive front. Cell intensities were averaged within 100 × 100 µm spatial blocks, and adjacent distance bins were compared (two-sided Mann-Whitney; Benjamini-Hochberg (BH); scale bar 200 µm). (c) Representative images of E-cadherin and SNAIL1-stained glandular, moderately/highly fragmented regions. Scale bar 100 µm. (d) Projected mean spatial-coherence score calculated for each tile, grouped by (i) homotypic and (ii) heterotypic cell pairs. Positive scores reflect stronger-than-random co-localization, whereas negative scores indicate spatial avoidance. Dot size scales with relative abundance of cell types. Box plot shows spatial-coherence of each tile across different pairs (n = 138 tiles from one patient; 41,477 tumour cells: 21,463 VIM-high and 20,014 ANXA1-high; paired Wilcoxon/BH). (e) Changes in spatial clusters (top) and architecture types (bottom) along pseudotime, profiled within consecutive sliding windows. (f) Tile-level U-Net embedding features projected into two dimensions and coloured by predicted architecture class. The overlaid PAGA trajectory depicts the inferred path through embedding space from glandular-like tiles toward fragmented/solid architectures (left). Architecture probabilities averaged across pseudotime bins along this trajectory (middle). Cell phenotype fractions were mapped onto the same pseudotime axis (right). All boxplots show median, IQR, 1.5×IQR whiskers.

(a) Boxplot (median, IQR, 1.5×IQR whiskers) representing nuclear shape descriptors (circularity and solidity) averaged per transcriptomic region for 249 tumour AOIs from 8 patients. Each dot represents one AOI (linear mixed-effects model with patient as a random intercept, contrasting fragmented architectures “fragmented and moderately fragmented” pooled against “solid, glandular dense, glandular, and glandular infiltrated” pooled classes; two-sided permutation tests stratified by patient to account for repeated tumour AOIs within patients, n.s. = not significant). (b) Dot plot of immune and stromal cell-type signature enrichment in GeoMx stroma AOIs across tumour architectures (n = 76 stroma AOIs from 6 patients). Each dot represents a cell-type gene signature (columns) within a given architecture (rows). Dot colour indicates the mean z-scored module score across AOIs, with red and blue denoting relative enrichment and depletion, respectively. Dot size reflects the percentage of AOIs with a z-score exceeding 0.5. Z-scores were computed across all stroma AOIs irrespective of architecture.

(a) UMAP of Leiden clusters from scRNA-seq data of 5 patient-derived CRC organoids cultured in Matrigel. (b) Correlation dotplots of single cells across entire dataset scored using CBC, Regenerative SC and EMT gene sets. (c) Dotplot of mean expression levels and % of expressing cells of selected cell state and identity marker genes across the cell lines. (d) Gene set enrichment analyses of β-catenin and YAP transcriptional targets across patient-derived organoids. (e) Representative top- and side-view and quantification of ANXA1-stained patient-derived organoids (line 2) from surface to invaginating architectures when grown in either high WNT or no WNT conditions (error bars = 95% CI; scale bars 50 µm; n = 3 independent experiments with 200 cells/condition/experiment from at least 3 structures; Two-way ANOVA/Dunnett’s) (f) RT-qPCR analysis of WNT target genes AXIN2 and ASCL2, normalized to B2M expression (mean±SD; n = 6 independent experiments; Student’s t-test/Welch’s). (g, h) Representative images and quantification of SOX4 (left) and β-catenin nuclear intensity in organoids treated with either DMSO or Chir for 4 days (mean; scale bars 20 µm; n = 3 independent experiments, Student’s t-test). (i) Treatment schematic, representative images and quantification of ANXA1 in organoids treated either with Chir or TDI-011536 (YAPa) or sequentially first with Chir then YAPa (scale bars 50 µm; n = 3 independent experiments, one-way ANOVA/Tukey’s). (j, k) Representative images and quantification of ANXA1 and SNAIL1 intensity (j) in mechanically compressed versus uncompressed organoids, as well as quantification of ANXA1 intensity binned by EMT status of the organoids (k) as defined by binary levels of SNAIL1 (box plots show min-to-max and mean; scale bars 30 µm; n = 3 independent experiments with >300 cells/condition/experiment; Student’s t-test (j); one-way ANOVA/Tukey’s (k)).

(a) UMAP of Leiden clusters from sc-RNAseq data of patient-derived organoids (line 2) treated with TDI-011536 (YAPa), TGF-β1 or both. (b) Density plots of the “hybrid state” cells across EMT-Regenerative SC state axis. Blue and red curves represent a 2-component Gaussian mixture model (GMM) fit of RegSC-and EMT-pole mode onto those values, with black curve marking GMM(2) sum. Vertical line marks per-dataset distribution mean μ_dist, together with d0 = μ_dist / SD. Number of hybrid cells and Cohen’s d between the two GMM components are indicated. (c) Quantification of SNAIL1 and ANXA1 intensities and their anticorrelation in YAPa, TGF-β1 or dual treated organoids (mean ±SD; n = 3 independent experiments; one-way ANOVA/Tukey’s). (d, e) Representative images (d) and quantification (e) of nuclear shape and DAPI periphery-to-centre ratio in YAPa- and TGF-β1-treated organoids (mean ±SD; scale bars 30 µm; n = 3 independent experiments; one-way ANOVA/Tukey’s). (f) Representative images and quantification of HP1α in YAPa- and TGF-β1-treated organoids (mean ±SD; scale bars 75 µm; n = 4 independent experiments; one-way ANOVA/Tukey’s). (g) Gene set enrichment analyses (CC = cellular component, BP = biological process, MF = molecular function) from spatial transcriptomics binned by architectures. (h) Z-score heatmap of chromatin regulator expression across architectures (i, j) Representative images (i) and quantification (j) of H3K9me2,3 in patient biopsies. Yellow dashed lines mark tumour-stroma boundary (scale bars 20 µm; n = 8 patients; two-sided patient-stratified permutation; Benjamini-Hochberg correction). (k) Nuclear circularity in patient biopsies across H3K9me2,3 intensity bins (n = 8 patients; two-way ANOVA/Dunnett’s). (l) Representative images of organoid transplants. Dotted lines outline visible tumours. (m) Representative images and quantification of pSMAD2/3 and active YAP (aYAP) from tumour xenografts (pSMAD2/3: n = 55 YAPa/64TGF-β1/ 66 Dual cells; aYAP: n = 95 YAPa/ 73 TGF-β1/112 Dual cells, pooled across >3 tumours/condition; one-way ANOVA/Tukey’s). (n) ANXA1 intensities in transplanted organoids (mean ±SD; n = 4 mice/condition; one-way ANOVA/Tukey’s). All boxplots show median, IQR, 1.5×IQR whiskers.

Live imaging of organoids. Patient-derived CRC organoids embedded in 1 mg ml−1 collagen gels treated with DMSO (control), LATS kinase inhibitor (YAPa), recombinant TGFβ1, or both recombinant TGFβ1 and LATS kinase inhibitor (YAPa +TGFβ1) and imaged every 30 min for 96  h on a bright-field microscope. Scale bar, 50 µm.

#1248. How Man United's data gurus got Leny Yoro off the hook: Stats analysis from ex-Formula One boffin proved Alexander Isak had NO chance of reaching the ball before red card - in appeal win that has left refs fuming

Published: 07:49 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 11:31 EST, 26 November 2026

Manchester United turned to its data gurus in a bid to categorically prove Alexander Isak had no chance of reaching the ball as part of its evidence to overturn Leny Yoro’s red card.

Yoro was sent off eight minutes into United’s trip to Anfield for a last-man foul on Isak, which referee Sam Barrott determined fit the criteria for Denial Of A Goalscoring Opportunity (DOGSO).

The young United centre-back was shown a straight red card after VAR doubled down on the day, insisting that no ‘clear and obvious error’ had been made.

United successfully appealed the decision through an independent panel and the lengths they went to for their evidence submission has now come to light.

Bosses at United included three high-definition video clips of the incident in question, which used multiple different angles as well as speeds in slow-motion and in real time for the panel to consider.

United also submitted video evidence of a DOGSO sending off earlier this season for Brighton’s Pascal Struijk against Sunderland, which was also overturned on appeal.

Leny Yoro was sent off for Man United against Liverpool but the red card was later rescinded

United showed that Isak would not have reached the ball if he'd have stayed on his feet

The most fascinating element of United’s detailed evidence pack came via its data department, led by ex-Formula One guru Michael Sansoni.

United outlined in a letter to the appeal panel that a technical analysis of the incident saw boffins at Carrington calculate the probability of Isak reaching the ball following his heavy touch prior to contact from Yoro.

The data allowed for the possibility that Isak maintained his speed and direction from the moment his legs first made contact with Yoro to assess whether he would have got to the ball before United goalkeeper Senne Lammens.

United’s analysis concluded that Isak would have been 1.8 metres shy of reaching the ball even if all optimal speed and directional factors had been achieved.

The appeals commission, however, told United that that data, however detailed, was not verifiable and so had to be treated with ‘caution’.

Considering all the elements of United’s submission, the panel unanimously agreed that it was not a red card offence and did not meet the threshold for DOGSO, immediately overturning the decision and withdrawing all punishment against Yoro.

‘We can accept referee can make a mistake. But we have VAR. What were they doing?’ a fuming Mauricio Pochettino said on Tuesday of the original Yoro decision.

‘We are going to repeat the game? Play similar tools the game XI v XI? We have an unbelievable car but we have to be at the level to drive. We accept the technology.’

#1247. Moyes Discusses Everton Team News For Merseyside Derby

David Moyes remained tight-lipped on his team news ahead of the 249th Merseyside derby, explaining Everton have "bits and pieces" going on when it comes to his squad's fitness.

The Blues host Liverpool at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Sunday (12pm GMT kick-off).

James Tarkowski definitely misses out, with the Everton captain serving the first of a three-match suspension after being shown a red card during the defeat at Brentford on Monday night.

When asked about other issues facing his side during Friday's pre-match press conference at Finch Farm, Moyes said: "We've got bits and pieces going on, which I'm sure every other team has as well."

On the absence of Tarkowski, Moyes added: "Tarky will be a miss because of his leadership and a lot of things he brings to the side, so we'll miss him, but, look, it's one position where we have got some cover so we're not short there.

"Michael Keane has been great form – any time he plays for us, he's played really well. He and Jake [O'Brien] are very much part of [the thinking]. We've got pretty good competition at centre-back and there'll be opportunities for one or both of those players in different games."

The Opposition

Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola will be without Conor Bradley, Hugo Ekitike and Giovanni Leoni for Sunday's game, while Cody Gakpo is also expected to miss out.

Victor Munoz and Ryan Gravenberch face late fitness tests.

#1246. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

Emery had warned his players of complacency against the Norwegian champions, but Villa took command from the start and were ahead after 23 minutes.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Champions League fixture as Aston Villa host Viking in the Midlands.

Villa made history in their previous home Champions League outing last week, thrashing Fenerbahce 6-0 to seal the club’s biggest-ever European win. #1245. Matchday Guide: Everton v Liverpool

Everton host Liverpool in the Merseyside derby on Sunday 29 November (12pm KO).

Some key information follows.

A comprehensive matchday guide to help supporters plan their matchday, including our extensive Travel Hub and more on food and drink, digital tickets, accessibility and what’s happening in and around Hill Dickinson Stadium, is available at evertonfc.com/matchday.

HELP US MAKE MATCHDAY ENJOYABLE FOR EVERYONE

We want everyone visiting Hill Dickinson Stadium to enjoy their matchday experience in a safe, welcoming and inclusive environment. All supporters have a part to play in making that happen.

Support with passion and respect

We encourage supporters to get behind the team, create a fantastic atmosphere and show respect for those around them.

Discrimination, tragedy chanting, abusive behaviour, entering the field of play, throwing objects and the possession or use of pyrotechnics, including smoke bombs and flares, have no place at our matches. Those responsible face lengthy stadium bans, potential police investigation and further legal action.

Supporters bringing flags, banners or other items into the stadium, or wearing clothing displaying messages, are reminded that these must not feature offensive, discriminatory or inflammatory content, including politically motivated or nationalistic messaging.

See it. Report it.

If you witness any anti-social behaviour, harassment, abuse or discrimination, please let us know. Supporters can report incidents confidentially by:

  • Speaking to a steward or police officer.
  • Texting HELP to 84300, along with details of the incident and its location.
  • Emailing reportit@evertonfc.com.

Reporting incidents at the time they occur helps our Stadium Safety Team respond more effectively.

Alcohol restrictions on Regent Road

Supporters attending Sunday’s fixture should be aware that a Public Spaces Protection Order issued by Liverpool City Council will be in place, prohibiting the consumption of alcohol in public spaces on Regent Road.

Keep your belongings safe

If you are driving to the match, please take a moment to ensure no valuables, cash, mobile devices or chargers are left on display in your vehicle.

Merseyside Police have advised that thieves are known to target vehicles parked by football supporters on matchdays at both Hill Dickinson Stadium, Goodison Park and Anfield. Taking a few simple precautions before heading to the stadium can help reduce the risk of becoming a victim of crime.

1878s FLAG AND BANNER DISPLAY

A flag and banner display will take place in the South Stand ahead of kick-off, with flags placed on selected seats across both the upper and lower tiers. Supporters are encouraged to wave them as the teams emerge from the tunnel.

Banners will also be draped from the North Stand upper.

After the game, please leave the flags under your seat so they can be collected by the fan volunteers and reused at future fixtures.

KEY TIMINGS

9am - Access to the stadium site opens via the Regent Road wall, with food and drink outlets on the Budweiser Plaza*. All available gates (A–E) in the Regent Road wall will be open and supporters are encouraged to use the full range of entrances to help avoid unnecessary congestion. 

9am - The Ticket Office also opens until half-time. The away ticket office, located outside the North Stand turnstiles, will also open at 9am.

10am - Stadium turnstiles open, with food and drink available across all concourses, including Early Bird offers until 11am. Please ensure your digital match ticket has been downloaded to your mobile device before arriving at the stadium. A step-by-step digital ticketing guide and stadium map can be found HERE.

12pm - Kick-off.

AFTER THE FULL-TIME WHISTLE

1.50pm - Following the end of the game, the South Stand Bar will remain open for two hours for home supporters, with Level 0 open to for 30 minutes (see below for more details).

In addition to the South Stand, bars on the Budweiser Plaza will remain open for approximately one hour after full-time, giving supporters the opportunity to stay for a drink before beginning their journey home.

NB: Supporters should leave Hill Dickinson Stadium using the designated exit gates (A–E) on the Regent Road wall. The Nelson Dock exit, accessed from the Budweiser Plaza, is reserved exclusively for supporters with allocated parking in this area, including supporters using accessible parking. Please note, there will be no pedestrian access from Nelson Dock onto Regent Road after the game. 

SOUTH STAND BAR OPENING (POST-MATCH)

The Upper South Stand bar will remain open for two hours for Evertonians after the final whistle.

All supporters on Level 2 can access this bar after the game and, subject to capacity and operational requirements, home supporters from lower areas will also be able to access the bar post-match. This will be via the Lower South escalators for fans on Level 0, or via pass gates at Entrance 7a if coming from other areas of the stadium.

#1244. The assist of the season! Remarkable new footage shows moment Bruno Fernandes created the divot HIMSELF before scoring one of the most bizarre goals EVER in Man United's chaotic draw with Sporting Lisbon

Published: 18:33 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:51 EST, 26 November 2026

Footage appears to show Bruno Fernandes created the divot in the turf that led to his fortunate second goal against Sporting Lisbon.

The Manchester United captain scored a bizarre goal against his former side on Wednesday night, with his long-range shot taking a fortuitous bobble off the Estadio Jose Alvalade pitch to leave goalkeeper Kaique Pereira helpless.

While fingers were initially pointed at the ground staff, footage shows the divot was actually created by Fernandes himself when he planted his boot into the turf while pressing high up the pitch moments earlier.

Reminiscent of former Liverpool forward Stan Collymore's famous bobbling goal past Blackburn Rovers goalkeeper Tim Flowers in 1996, Fernandes' speculative effort would undoubtedly have been easily gathered by Pereira had it not struck the bump in the turf.

The goal summed up another chaotic evening for United, in which goalkeeping calamities, controversial refereeing calls, three penalties and a red card resulted in a 2-2 draw and left them 19th in the Champions League standings.

United trailed at the break after goalkeeper Senne Lammens saved one penalty before conceding another 75 seconds later that was converted by Luis Suarez after the Belgian's reckless challenge on Max Araujo.

"This is the assist of the season" 😅Bruno Fernandes created the divot in the turf which led to his second goal of the evening for Man Utd 🪄📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/c4g2sC33pA

Fernandes' speculative effort would undoubtedly have been easily gathered by Pereira had it not struck the bump in the turf

The visitors were left furious when Amad Diallo saw a first-half leveller ruled out after referee Szymon Marciniak blew his whistle too early for VAR to intervene, but United turned the game around shortly after the restart.

Lisandro Martinez, who had given away the first penalty, won one at the other end that Fernandes converted before the former Sporting star fired in the long-range effort that bounced over Pereira and into the net.

More drama followed as Lammens flapped at a cross under pressure from Suarez, allowing the striker to score, before Patrick Dorgu was adjudged to have put undue pressure on Pereira when forcing an own goal from the goalkeeper.

United were left frustrated by what they viewed as a lack of consistency after Marciniak was sent to the pitchside monitor to review the second decision, and their mood darkened further when Youri Tielemans was sent off for a second booking late on.

Former United player Ashley Young claimed that 2022 World Cup referee Marciniak's decision-making during the clash was a 'disgrace'.

Young told BBC Radio 5 Live: 'The referee’s performance was just simply wow. The decisions that he gave.

'Youri Tielemans getting booked to eventually getting sent off later because you booked him when it should never have been a booking and it should have been an equalising goal.

'The third goal that should have stood because he’s saying Patrick Dorgu fouled the keeper. The keeper comes out and flaps at it before he is even touched. How that has gone to VAR is beyond me.

'His decision-making is nothing more than a disgrace.'

Former United player Ashley Young claimed that 2022 World Cup referee Marciniak's decision-making during the clash was a 'disgrace'

Young’s former United team-mate Rio Ferdinand echoed that frustration on X.

Writing alongside a pain image of himself, he said with two emojis indicating angry swearing: 'REFEREE. What have I just witnessed tonight!

'Regardless – individual mistakes again proving costly. Positives to take from tonight, recharge the batteries!'

In what is proving to be an eventful first week in charge, Pochettino was asked to provide his assessment of the game. The Argentine said: 'It depends which way you prefer (to analyse the game). So proud of the players. It was a very tough game. I like the team for the 90 minutes, the personality, the character.

'We showed the way we want to play. We've only been working together one week.'

But, he added: 'Always we need to concentrate more and focus more. Try to recover better. We start to fix. With a performance like today it's the best medicine to prepare the next game.'

United have little time to take stock before their next outing, with Brentford visiting Old Trafford on Saturday.

#1243. Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

A brilliantly worked team-goal finished off by Declan Rice, and Arsenal are level 💥 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Y25zI80A0z

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

Manchester United are now 4-0 down against a Como team managed by Cesc Fabregas. There is still 15 minutes or more to play. You can follow the rest of the game here to see if they can stem the bleeding.

Will the substitutes again make the difference for Arsenal tonight? In each of their last three league victories, they have won because of goals scored by substitutes. This speaks to the quality of Arteta’s squad, obviously, but also to the Arsenal manager’s ability to pick the right players for the right moments. Over the last year or so, this has become a real strength.

Karl had been expected to replace Olise on the right, but Kompany looks to have stiffened up his midfield by starting Pavlovic, Laimer and Bischof. It will be interesting to see how Saibari and Kane dovetail, two stick-on strikers. It is not Bayern’s strongest team, with Luis Diaz also on the bench.

Bayern Munich starting XI: Neuer, Stanisic, Kim Minjae, Upamecano, Davies, Pavlovic, Laimer, Bischof, Gnabry, Saibari, Kane

Subs: UIreich, Urbig, Ito, Tah, Brown, Luis Diaz, Boey, Sapoko Ndiaye, Karl, Binder

There was little doubt that Arteta would view this game as one that suits Jurrien Timber rather than Ben White. Arsenal’s manager has changed tack by starting Calafiori, who was rested for Arsenal’s first two Champions League games, but Bayern at the Allianz is a significant step up in grade. Madueke rewarded for his showing at Forest.

Arsenal XI: Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Rice, Guimaraes, Odegaard; Saka, Havertz, Madueke

Subs: Kepa, Meslier, White, Mosquera, Lewis-Skelly, Zubimendi Merino, Eze, Gyokeres, Dowman

🔵 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 🟡 Two changes for tonight's test ✊

Vincent Kompany is in the building. It wasn’t clear whether the Bayern head coach would be able to attend tonight’s game because he’s been battling a nasty virus over the last few days. He did not do the usual pre-match press conference yesterday but clearly feels well enough to be here tonight.

In an extract from Sam Dean’s new book on Arsenal’s resurgence under the Spaniard, he reveals that Mike Ashley was keen to bring Arteta to Newcastle United in 2019.

Sam writes: “Arteta also did not have a coaching staff assembled. It is believed that he tried to bring some key individuals on board, such was his interest in accepting Newcastle’s offer, but that the timing was not right for the people he truly wanted. In the end, much to the frustration of Newcastle and Ashley, he said no.”

Arsenal: The Inside Story of Arsenal’s Rebirth Under Mikel Arteta (Pan Macmillan, RRP £22).

This is a proper heavyweight clash but, sadly for the neutrals watching, Bayern are missing some big players. Michael Olise is suspended, Jamal Musiala is injured and Joshua Kimmich is unavailable following the death of his father.

This should all work in Arsenal’s favour, and Mikel Arteta will be looking for a repeat of the energy and quality that his team showed against Bayern last season. Arsenal won 3-1 at the Emirates in November in a performance of real class. It was arguably their most complete showing of the entire campaign.

Ice cold from Martinelli 🥶 https://t.co/uQEHb4x7eH

Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

#1242. SFA are told to think again by clubs as latest youth plans are kicked into touch

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 13:49 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 14:19 EST, 26 November 2026

The SFA have been forced back to the drawing board for a second time in their efforts to introduce new proposals around youth development.

Led by chief football officer Craig Mulholland, the plans had been geared towards ensuring more Under-21 players in Scotland gain more minutes at first-team level.

The original plans were for two Scotland-eligible Under-21 players to start in domestic cup competitions, and for players to feature for a minimum of six per cent of all available minutes across a season in league campaigns.

When it became clear that several clubs in Scotland weren’t on board, a new watered-down version was put back on the table.

But the new proposals have also now been met with resistance — forcing the SFA to kick the can further down the road into the new year.

There will now be no vote on the back of the upcoming AGM, with further discussions required prior to something more concrete coming to fruition for the start of next season.

SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland has been sent back to the drawing board by clubs

A statement from the governing body said: ‘The Scottish FA has been encouraged by the productive dialogue with clubs regarding proposals to harness opportunities for young homegrown talent.

‘The most recent discussions have spawned a range of additional potential innovations that all parties agree will require further consultation in order to present a consolidated package of recommendations to an SPFL member vote.

‘The passion we all have for Scottish football has been demonstrated by the public debate sparked since the all-club meeting in St Andrews, when the reality of our domestic game’s standing in respect of playing time for under-21 players compared to the rest of Europe was made clear.

‘We will continue to engage in dialogue with the aim of delivering a proposal that will achieve the stated objective of improving opportunities for young homegrown players to fulfil their potential at the top end of the Scottish professional game.

‘It is an objective everyone benefits from: players, clubs, supporters and Scotland national teams.

‘We have therefore agreed that the consultation process will continue into the New Year with the intention of a comprehensive proposal going to SPFL members within the first quarter of 2027, in time for the start of William Hill SPFL season 2027-28.

‘The Scottish FA General Meeting to vote on the complementary Scottish Gas Men’s Scottish Cup proposals will now follow a similar timetable.

‘Given the implications for our game, and our young talent, it is imperative that we take the necessary time to get those proposals right.’

Crystal Palace defender Chris Richards has confirmed that discussions over a new contract are underway, with the American international considering his options as uncertainty surrounds his long-term future at Selhurst Park.

The 26-year-old has established himself as an important member of the Eagles’ defensive setup since arriving from Bayern Munich in 2022, but his current agreement is nearing its end.

Speaking ahead of Crystal Palace’s Europa League meeting with Real Sociedad, Richards confirmed that negotiations with the club are ongoing and suggested that extending his stay remains a realistic possibility.

According to a report via SoccerNews, the defender’s current contract expires in the summer of 2027, although the Eagles reportedly have an option to extend it by another year.

Richards admitted he is carefully considering what is best for both his career and the club, indicating that an agreement has yet to be reached.

“There’s always a possibility of extending. We’ve been speaking with the club. I’m just trying to figure out what’s right for my career, and what’s right for the club.”

The United States international has made 138 appearances for Palace, scoring five goals, and has played an important role in their recent success.

He was part of the squad that enjoyed a memorable period under Oliver Glasner, winning the FA Cup, Community Shield and Europa League.

Richards also acknowledged how much his time at Selhurst Park has contributed to his development, thanking the club for helping him progress as a footballer.

The defender believes Palace have achieved significant milestones in recent years and would welcome the opportunity to experience further success in European competitions.

However, he made it clear that his immediate priority is helping the team improve their results before returning to discussions about his future.

Richards recently reached 100 Premier League appearances, underlining his growing importance at the highest level.

Palace will certainly want to avoid losing an established defensive option on a free transfer, particularly given his experience and potential.

Much will depend on whether both parties can agree on the financial and sporting terms of a new contract in the coming months.

#1240. Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Although coronary artery disease (CAD) genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci, most variants lie in non-coding regions, obscuring the causal gene programmes and cell types driving disease1,2. Here we performed single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility in human coronary arteries from 44 people to construct a genome-wide single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map. We identified 11,269 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) across principal vascular cell types, including CAD-associated caQTLs in smooth muscle cells (SMCs). Using dynamic single-cell caQTL modelling3, we show that variant effects on chromatin vary across SMC states. For example, rs658956-mediated suppression of the FGGY-DT enhancer through disruption of an AP-1 motif is amplified as SMCs transition towards a fibromyocyte fate. We next performed genome-wide high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) in 15 human coronary arteries, showing that rs4887091 in the ADAMTS7 CAD locus has allele-dependent effects on CCCTC-binding factor occupancy and loop strength. Integrating Hi-C, Hi-C with chromatin immunoprecipitation and in vitro clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats interference (CRISPRi) nominated AMOTL2 as a distal SMC-specific CAD gene whose loss promotes proliferation and suppresses contractile identity. Finally, arrayed Perturb–seq of GWAS-nominated enhancers converged on extracellular matrix remodelling as a core SMC disease programme. Together, these findings provide a framework for mapping non-coding GWAS variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

Common diseases are driven by a multitude of factors and remain difficult to treat given the lack of a unified disease mechanism4. Coronary artery disease (CAD) is among the most prevalent common chronic diseases, and numerous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have now identified hundreds of variants linked to CAD risk. Although these results may potentially pave the way for new therapeutic target discovery1,2,5,6, much of the translation from GWAS to therapeutic targets for CAD has been restricted to lipid-lowering drugs7,8. Large-scale clinical studies have demonstrated a persistent residual risk of CAD independent of lipid levels9,10, but we lack drugs that directly target disease pathways in the vessel wall due to an incomplete understanding of causal disease mechanisms. Leveraging human genetics to uncover new lipid-independent biological mechanisms and drug targets in CAD represents a tremendous unmet need and would be a principal milestone in translating population-scale GWAS findings to therapies for patients11,12.

Although population-scale GWAS offer great opportunity for target discovery, most identified variants lie within non-coding regions of the genome, making it difficult to dissect the causal cell types and molecular pathways13. The advent of single-cell sequencing technologies now allows for the profiling of human tissues in health and disease at unprecedented granularity14. Previous studies have used traditional single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) for detailed characterization of cell states in human tissue that drive disease15,16,17,18; however, these studies do not profile the non-coding genome, making it challenging to link GWAS variants to observed molecular changes. More recently, single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) with sequencing (snATAC–seq) in human coronary arteries was conducted to link CAD GWAS variants to regulatory elements19. Although this represented an important advance in the field, the lack of complementary transcriptomic profiling rendered it challenging to nominate causal genes in vascular cell types. Furthermore, isolated snATAC–seq precludes the discovery of distal gene regulation as a driver of disease20, and there are currently no studies that profile the three-dimensional (3D) chromatin architecture in human coronary arteries to enable the investigation of these distal regulatory connections.

Herein we performed simultaneous multi-omic profiling of the transcriptome and epigenome in nuclei from 44 human coronary arteries to build a multi-omic enhancer–gene map of CAD. Collectively, these analyses identified CAD-associated regulatory variants and enhancer–gene links in smooth muscle cells (SMCs), motivating focused analysis of SMC state-dependent gene regulation. To expand insight into gene regulation across functionally heterogeneous SMC cell states, we used dynamic chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTL) modelling to uncover cell-state-dependent pathogenicity of disease variants. To dissect the role of disease-associated variants in regulating larger scale gene networks, we performed genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries to link variants to distal genes and validated our findings using cell-specific high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) with chromatin immunoprecipitation (Hi-ChIP–seq) and in vitro CRISPRi. Finally, we performed Perturb–seq in human coronary artery SMCs (HCASMCs) to characterize functional mechanisms of repressing disease-associated enhancers and genes. Collectively, we provide a multi-omic map of human CAD by integrating transcriptomic, epigenetic and chromatin architecture to link disease-associated genetic variants with candidate disease-relevant cell types and target genes.

We performed single-nucleus Multi-ome (RNA+ATAC) sequencing in 44 human coronary arteries from non-failing donors and patients with chronic heart failure isolated at the time of heart transplantation (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). After quality control, we recovered 126,804 nuclei from 11 distinct cell types (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 1b–d). Using differential expression of canonical genes, we identified clusters corresponding to all main vascular cell types, including coronary artery SMCs (MYH11, ACTA2, ITGA8), endothelial cells (VWF, LDB2, PECAM1), fibroblasts (LAMA2, DCN, FBLN1) and myeloid cells (F13A1, CD163, MRC1) (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Table 2). We used MACS2 to identify areas of open chromatin (‘peaks’) from the ATAC–seq data (Fig. 1e) and identified 143,743 cell-type-specific differentially accessible peaks (Extended Data Fig. 1d,e). Generally, cell-type clustering was concordant between the RNA and ATAC data. However, gene-expression data enabled the annotation of rarer cell types that were not captured by ATAC-based clustering alone (Supplementary Fig. 1e–g). Using differentially accessible peaks across cells, we also discovered cell-type-specific enrichment of transcriptional motifs such as SpiB and PU.1 in myeloid cells, MEF2B/C/D in SMCs and CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein in adipocytes (Supplementary Fig. 1h). We linked peaks to genes using a new supervised single-cell model called single-cell enhancer-to-gene (E2G) (scE2G)21 (Fig. 1d, Extended Data Fig. 2a–g and Supplementary Tables 3–14; Methods). We found that the non-immune cells had the greatest number of shared enhancers relative to myeloid cells (Fig. 1d) and that all cell types had a similar number of E2G links (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 3).

a, Study design. b, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding plot of integrated data clustered by RNA. c, Cell-type composition stack plot by sample. NK, natural killer. d, Number of shared enhancers heatmap (right) from scE2G map (left); defined as the number of enhancers where more than 50% of the peak width overlaps with other cell type-specific peaks. e, Number of scE2G links in the main cell types. f, Linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) for cardiometabolic traits by cell type; dotted line, multiple-testing-adjusted P value threshold. P values were calculated using one-sided stratified LDSC, with Bonferroni correction for six conditions (P < 8.33 × 10−3). Illustrations in a and d created in BioRender: a, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/ib7ak3x (2026); d, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/cwi31gk (2026).

Notably, we found that cardiometabolic disease variants for CAD, systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were enriched in differentially accessible marker peaks specific to SMCs and endothelial cells (Fig. 1f). As a predominantly non-vascular trait, diabetes did not demonstrate enrichment of disease-associated variants (Fig. 1f).

To boost our power for single-cell caQTL (sc-caQTL) discovery, we integrated our Multi-ome ATAC–seq data with available snATAC–seq data from human coronary arteries19 to create a meta-map of 88 samples and 245,562 nuclei across four ancestry groups (Extended Data Fig. 3a–f). We then used RASQUAL to identify pseudobulk caQTLs in four principal vascular cell types (SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells, fibroblasts) (Fig. 2a). At the 10% false discovery rate (FDR) threshold, we found 11,269 significant caQTL associations in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3g–i, Supplementary Fig. 2a–d and Supplementary Tables 15–26). Power, sensitivity, subsampling and runtime analyses are shown in Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3 and described in Supplementary Methods.

a, Schematic of sc-caQTL discovery with disease enrichment. b, Number of sc-caQTLs by cell type at FDR 0.05. c, Regional Manhattan plot of CAD GWAS1 and SMC caQTL results at the rs658956 locus. d, snATAC–seq tracks with E2G link centred at the rs658956 locus showing SMC-specific enrichment of the enhancer with an E2G link to FGGY-DT. e, Violin plot showing normalized expression by genotype for rs658956 and FGGY-DT in coronary arteries from GTEx (P = 3.39 × 10−12). The P value was calculated using a two-sided t-test of the GTEx eQTL linear regression coefficient against zero. f, PRINT and seq2PRINT transcription factor binding prediction pipeline (left). rs658956 overlaps region with high transcription factor binding probability from seq2PRINT model (top) and multiscale footprinting associates rs658956 with a transcription factor-specific footprint (bottom). g, Motif analysis finds rs658956 overlaps canonical AP-1 transcription factor (JUN, FOS) motifs. Ref, reference alelle; Alt, alternate allele. h, EMSA demonstrates a binding shift in the reference allele sequence (containing G) that was not present in the alternative allele sequence (containing T) when these allelic sequences were exposed to nuclear lysate from SMCs (n = 3 replicates, representative experiment shown). i, Dynamic caQTL modelling and discovery strategy (cell-state-dependent). j, rs658956 caQTL dynamic effect size. Net effect size depicted here represents the sum of \({\beta }_{g}\) and \({\beta }_{{\rm{F}}{\rm{M}}{\rm{C}}{\rm{x}}{\rm{G}}}\) in our generalized linear mixed model across cells. k, rs658956 genotype association with normalized chromatin accessibility across FMC tertiles. Negative slope of association increases as FMC score increases; n = 268 (e) and n = 79 (k) biologically independent samples were used. Illustrations in a and i created in BioRender: a, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/cwi31gk (2026); i, Lavine, K. https://biorender.com/m3r2gap (2026).

We further characterized caQTL variants to assess their regulatory potential. Lead caQTL variants were enriched strongly near the peaks they were predicted to regulate, consistent with a cis-regulatory mechanism (Extended Data Fig. 3j). We next overlapped our pseudobulk caQTLs and GTEx bulk arterial tissue eQTLs by cell type and found several hundred shared QTL variants in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3i). Furthermore, we found a strong correlation in effect size between our SMC caQTLs and bulk coronary artery eQTLs from GTEx (Extended Data Fig. 3k). Finally, in SMCs we trained a convolutional neural net model (seq2PRINT22) that incorporates chromatin accessibility and ATAC footprinting to predict transcription factor binding probability at a base-pair resolution. We found that caQTL variants within accessible peaks had significantly higher predicted transcription factor binding probabilities compared with all other non-caQTL SNP sites within accessible peaks (P = 8.2 × 10−40, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Extended Data Fig. 3l).

To identify disease-associated caQTLs, we overlapped sc-caQTLs for each cell type with CAD GWAS variants (defined as lead variants associated with CAD at 1% FDR1 and variants in linkage disequilibrium with these at R2 ≥ 0.8 in the European population from 1000 Genomes Project; Supplementary Table 27), which yielded numerous disease-relevant cell-type-specific caQTLs (Extended Data Fig. 3m). For example, we found that rs7182567 was an SMC-specific caQTL that was also a GWAS variant (P = 5.4 × 10−26) and a bulk GTEx eQTL for ADAMTS7 in tibial artery (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Similarly, we found that rs8017642 is an endothelial cell-specific caQTL in the NEK9 locus (Extended Data Fig. 4b), whereas rs2337154 and rs1443120 are fibroblast- and myeloid-specific caQTLs, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d).

Next, we leveraged the paired RNA data to sub-cluster SMCs into transcriptionally distinct cell states, forming a continuum from ‘healthy’ contractile SMC states (SMC1–3) to de-differentiated ‘disease-associated’ SMC states including fibromyocytes (FMCs) and chondromyocytes (CMCs) (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Notably, we found that ADAMTS7 was expressed most highly in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 4e), indicating a role in disease regulation. To identify functionally distinct endothelial cell states, we mapped our data to a high-resolution scRNA-seq atherosclerosis atlas23 and identified four transcriptionally distinct endothelial subsets (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Notably, NEK9 was expressed in endothelial cells enriched with endothelium-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes such as COL1A1 and FN1 (refs. 24,25) (Extended Data Fig. 4f,g). Pathway enrichment in the EMT population showed increased EMT and stress-response signals (Extended Data Fig. 4h). Next, we created a gene set score comprised of 41 endothelial cell-specific genes thought to be associated causally with CAD26 that showed maximal enrichment in intimal endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Similarly, we created a gene signature of a gene programme26 identified previously as driving CAD pathogenesis in endothelial cells (Programme 8) and found an enrichment of this programme in angiogenic and/or vasa vasorum endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4j).

The CAD disease-associated variant rs658956 illustrates how a cell-type-specific caQTL can impart functional transcriptional changes. The variant is an SMC-specific and fibroblast-specific caQTL and regulates a putative enhancer element (chr. 1: 59169569–59170069), which is linked to the gene FGGY-DT in an SMC-specific manner by scE2G (Fig. 2c,d). Consistently, we found that rs658956 is also a coronary artery eQTL for FGGY-DT expression (P = 3.4 × 10−12) wherein the alternative allele (T) is associated with decreased expression relative to the reference allele (G) (Fig. 2e) and is also predicted to overlie a high probability transcription factor binding site (Fig. 2f). Motif-based transcription factor binding site analysis found that rs658956 is predicted to disrupt a core AP-1 (JUN/FOS) transcription factor binding motif (5′-TGAGTCA-3′) (Fig. 2g). Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) demonstrated a binding shift in the reference allele sequence (containing G) that was not present in the alternative allele sequence (containing T) when these alleles were exposed to nuclear lysate from SMCs (Fig. 2h). Antibody supershift EMSA confirmed that the shifted AP-1 complex band consists of JUN and FOS transcription factors (Extended Data Fig. 4k). Together, these results suggest that the disease-associated variant rs658956 impacts transcription factor binding, thereby decreasing the chromatin accessibility of the enhancer and subsequently reducing FGGY-DT expression in a SMC-specific manner.

In atherosclerosis, SMCs undergo a well-characterized phenotypic switch from a contractile state to a fibroblast-like FMC phenotype16, driven by disease-associated transcriptional programmes. To characterize this transition, individual nuclei were assigned an FMC score based on FMC state marker genes for downstream modelling (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 5a–d). Notably, this FMC gene score is dynamic with disease across species, disease burden, pseudotime trajectory, in vitro HCASMC stress and transcriptional regulation (Extended Data Fig. 5e–k). To identify state-dependent caQTL effects, we used a Poisson mixed-effects (PME) single-cell model (Extended Data Fig. 6a–c; Methods). Applying this PME model to the lead variants of SMC-specific pseudobulk caQTLs, we identified 712 caQTLs whose effects were dynamic with respect to the FMC score (FDR ≤ 5%) (Supplementary Tables 29 and 30). Notably, eight of these dynamic caQTLs were also disease-associated variants. For example, rs658956 exhibited a significant interaction with FMC score (FDR-adjusted likelihood ratio test (LRT) P value = 2.36 × 10−4) (Fig. 2j,k). A negative interaction term indicates that, as the FMC score increased, the negative association between rs658956 and local chromatin accessibility was amplified (Fig. 2j,k). Using the scE2G map to link dynamic caQTL-related enhancer elements (caPeaks) to target genes, we found that extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling was the most enriched pathway among linked genes (Extended Data Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Table 31). Notably, several of these genes linked to dynamic caPeaks were enriched in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 32). Similar state-dependent effects were observed at other CAD loci such as dynamic caQTL variant rs11838776 in the COL4A1 locus, suggesting that COL4A1 may play a role during transition toward an FMC state (Extended Data Fig. 6g–k). Collectively, these dynamic analyses demonstrate that disease-associated variants can exert cell-state-dependent regulatory effects on chromatin accessibility.

To map CAD disease-associated variants to cell types and genes in an unbiased fashion, we built a disease-relevant single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map (scV2E2G) integrating cell-type-specific regulatory elements, CAD GWAS variants, scE2G links and caQTLs21,27 (Fig. 3a; Methods).

Links also supported by caQTLs: SMCs (56 genes), endothelial cells (8), fibroblasts (13) and myeloid cells (27).
