#1197. Ben Jacobs Names 3 Right-Backs Arsenal Are Targeting In January Transfer Window

Arsenal do not traditionally use the January transfer window to do lots of business, but this season may be different.

The Gunners sit pretty at the top of the Premier League table, six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City who sit second and third currently.

But they may look to strengthen their squad when the winter window opens and manager Mikel Arteta is targeting a right-back and a central midfielder.

GIVEMESPORT senior football correspondent Ben Jacobs believes the Gunners will look in the market in January, but may wait until the summer of 2027 to add significantly to their ranks.

Arsenal have suffered with a number of injuries already this season, with William Saliba and Jurrien Timber missing the start of the campaign, while Bukayo Saka, Martin Zubimendi and more recently David Raya are now sidelined.

Timber has had to cover at centre-back on occasions this season, with Ben White playing at right-back and it is therefore no surprise that they are potentially looking at reinforcements in the full-back area.

And Jacobs has named three potential targets in his exclusive GMS newsletter.

He said: "My information is that Arsenal will be looking for another midfielder, but before we talk about that particular area, we have to think about other pressing positions that Arsenal may focus on.

"As far as the winter is concerned, right-back is relatively high in Arsenal’s thinking, so maybe in the winter, they explore that, if not, it’ll be summer 2027. So yes, midfielder is important, and that is even after the arrival of Bruno Guimaraes, but right-back is another area.

"Arsenal are one of the clubs that have looked historically at Malo Gusto, along with Manchester City and even Manchester United in weeks gone by, but the challenge for all three of these clubs is price. £75million was what Chelsea wanted over the summer. If that drops, and Gusto becomes a market opportunity, then there’s several clubs, including from within England, that might decide to advance on Gusto. City were maybe the most concrete on Gusto over the summer, but nothing developed, as I say, because Chelsea’s asking price was just a little bit too high.

"You’ve got David Boly and also Ivan Fresneda, two players that are on Arsenal’s radar too, so they’ll be in the market for some form of right-back, for sure.”

#1196. Man United launch new matchday mental health and suicide prevention hub at OId Trafford for Brentford clash

Published: 06:19 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 08:02 EST, 27 November 2026

Manchester United will launch a new matchday mental health and suicide prevention initiative at Saturday’s game against Brentford at Old Trafford.

Working with the Premier League and Talk About It Mate, a support group based in Salford, United will host 10 sessions of The Check-In this season aimed at providing a welcoming space where supporters can drop in to talk with trained counsellors and volunteers.

Rhys Bennett, who was the captain of United's last FA Youth Cup-winning team in 2022, has spoken about the benefits of a recent Talk About It Mate session at Salford Lads Club. Bennett’s father David tragically took his own life last year.

‘It’s probably the most powerful thing I’ve ever done,’ said Bennett. ‘I’ve never done anything like this before. It’s made me feel even better than I did when I came in the door two hours ago. I’ve enjoyed every minute of it.

‘My dad passed at 51 and I think he grew up in the, “you’ll be alright, just crack on” (generation). He was an honest working man, and he went about his daily business until it became too much for him.

‘For him it would have been a really important thing to get things off his chest. A judgement free zone. It would have helped him massively. People are sharing the same experiences, people sat in a circle all going through different things.

Manchester United will launch a new matchday mental health and suicide prevention initiative at Saturday’s game against Brentford at Old Trafford

Rhys Bennett (right), who was the captain of United's last FA Youth Cup-winning team in 2022, attended a recent Talk About It Mate session at Salford Lads Club

‘To be honest, I was a little bit nervous. I'm not a nervous kind of person, but I think within five minutes, it's just no judgment and having that full confidence in being able to talk about how I'm really feeling.

‘I'm coming up for a year of my dad's passing. My dad committed suicide, and I played football for a living. I think it's hard navigating through being in a high-pressure environment.

‘I think it is the judgment thing, and not wanting to burden other people. But I think it's so important that you realise that most of the time it's not a burden.’

Bennett, who made a permanent move to Fleetwood in the summer and played in the League Two club’s shock Carabao Cup win over Arsenal last month, added: ‘You put the brave face on, and I feel weaker. But the more I talk about it, and the more I let my emotions out, that definitely does make me stronger in day-to-day life.

‘I used to just shut it out because I'm rocking up on a Saturday and a Tuesday in front of fans, and I've got to perform, and I feel everything. You get the adrenaline and everything of a football match, and then I'm back down to square one.

‘Just how open everyone was and how open I could be myself, really did surprise me. There wasn’t at any point that I couldn’t share something I was feeling. Everything came from the heart, it was really authentic and really powerful.’

Running five weekly men’s groups across Salford and with more than 1,000 group sessions delivered, Talk About It Mate creates spaces where men can connect, share experiences and support one another.

With a community-led approach to improving mental health and well-being, the organisation helps men build connections and reduce isolation.

United will host 10 sessions of The Check-In this season aimed at providing a welcoming space where supporters can drop in to talk with trained counsellors and volunteers

Bennett, whose father David tragically took his own life last year, spoke about how the session gave him 'full confidence in being able to talk about how I'm really feeling'

Man United say their partnership with Talk About It Mate will provide a welcoming space where supporters can access help on matchdays

Mike Richard, founder of Talk About It Mate, said: ‘We've spent years creating spaces where men feel safe enough to open up, and we're proud to be working with Manchester United to bring that approach to supporters.

‘Football has an incredible ability to bring people together, but being surrounded by thousands of people doesn't necessarily mean you feel connected. We know that some of the most important conversations can start in ordinary, familiar places – that's the kind of environment we want to create at Old Trafford.

‘This isn't about waiting until someone reaches crisis point. It's about making conversations around mental health a normal part of everyday life.’

According to The Samaritans, 5,738 suicides were registered in England in 2025, which equates to 11.1 deaths per 100,000 people.

The male suicide rate was 17.2 per 100,000 – compared to 5.4 per cent among females – with men aged 50-54 having the highest rate of any population group.

Rachel Fraser, United’s internal communications and inclusion director, said: ‘Our fans give so much to this club, and ensuring they feel supported in return is incredibly important to us.

‘Through our partnership with Talk About It Mate, we are proud to provide a welcoming space where supporters can access help on matchdays.

‘Football creates friendships and communities for fans that span generations. The Check-In builds on that sense of connection and seamlessly fits into the matchday routine, providing a safe and accessible space for those needing support.’

If you are affected by any of the issues raised in this article, please call the Samaritans for free on 116123.

#1195. Malagò insists Italy players pushed for Mancini’s return

Giovanni Malagò says Italy’s players were behind his decision to bring Roberto Mancini back as coach, and believes the Azzurri can rebuild around their young talent.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, the FIGC commissioner and presidential candidate was speaking at a debate organised by La Stampa at the MAUTO museum in Turin.

Malagò took charge of Italian football after the national team failed to reach a third consecutive World Cup, beaten by Bosnia and Herzegovina in March. He then turned to Mancini, who had won Euro 2020 in his first spell in charge.

“A federation president has to listen to everyone, but then the moment comes when it’s my face on the line,” Malagò said. “There’s an unwritten rule that if you don’t go to the World Cup, you go home. If we go out against Bosnia, it means we’re not exactly phenomenal.

“There aren’t years to plan and programme. I chose Mancini because I know his ideas about young players, and I speak with the national team players, who tell me: ‘Mancini all the way.’”

Italy’s Nations League campaign ended in disappointment. Despite beating France 3-1, the Azzurri lost 4-1 in Belgium and failed to progress. Malagò still sees reasons for optimism.

“We have to rebuild around young players. We had a great Nations League group. We lost to Belgium, but there’s light at the end of the tunnel,” he said.

“The senior team is only the peak of the movement, and Italy’s Under-21 side is very strong. We haven’t been to the Olympics with the Under-21s since 2008, and we’ve already laid all the right foundations to go back.”

The FIGC presidential election takes place in just over two weeks, with Malagò facing former Milan executive Adriano Galliani.

#1194. Ben Jacobs Shares Update on Liverpool Signing Lamine Camara in January

Liverpool are looking to strengthen their squad in the January transfer window, and Ben Jacobs has shared an update on their interest in bringing in a midfielder.

The Reds made three signings in the summer by bringing in Ronald Araujo, Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola, and the team have started the season well with the team sitting fourth in the Premier League, and having lost just three times in all competitions.

But Andoni Iraola is understood to be keen to strengthen his squad further for the second half of the season, and midfield additions are believed to be among the priority deals being targeted.

During the summer, the club were attentive to the situation regarding Lamine Camara, but a deal never materialised for them to make a move. However, GIVEMESPORT exclusively revealed that when Chelsea made a push to bring him in on Deadline Day, Liverpool made contact with the Senegal international to express their interest too.

“And then just final word on Lamine Camara, like I said on deadline day exclusively, Liverpool were calling Camara on deadline day, and they were saying, 'If you don’t go to Chelsea, we could be there for you in 2027'," he said.

"And Liverpool privately, according to my information, were very glad that Camara and Chelsea fell through, and it seems like now Chelsea want Alex Scott. Unless they get a big concession on the deal, it might be difficult for Chelsea to go back to Monaco and sign Camara, because the club relationship is a bit broken because Monaco didn’t send that deal to a deal sheet.

"Chelsea were really disappointed by Monaco’s handling there, which means if they are to renegotiate for Camara and move away from Alex Scott, they would likely need Monaco to make a significant concession, and that club-to-club relationship is still very difficult.”

With lots of interest in Camara during the summer window, Monaco boss Filipe Luis was asked about his midfielder and the speculation around his future, where he admitted that he didn't want to lose him, while calling him 'one of the best midfielders in the world'.

"We are probably talking about one of the best midfielders in the world," he said.

"I don't want to talk about him too much, because I know a lot of clubs would love to have him in their squad, and he is very important to me.

"He has that quality on the ball, covers a lot of ground, he is truly top class! I am really happy to have him, and he is going to play a key role in the team.

"Keeping him? I am very hopeful he will stay. I think he is happy in Monaco. So if he stays, he can play a key role in my game plan."

With the Ligue 1 outfit currently struggling domestically this season, it's unlikely that they will want to sell mid-season. However, their financial situation means that a good offer may force their hand, and Liverpool have the cash to spend if they deem it necessary.

Chelsea are seemingly out of the race as they chase a deal for Alex Scott instead, leaving the Reds with a clear run to bring in someone they see as a top target.

#1193. Rare gene variants can affect a person’s height by up to 17 centimetres

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chris Simms is a science writer based in Somerset, UK.

Human height is determined almost entirely by an individual’s DNA.Credit: XinXinXing/Getty

Rare mutations that prevent proteins from functioning can have a surprisingly large effect on people’s height, researchers have found.

An analysis of more than 1.4 million people’s protein-coding DNA has identified hundreds of genes that affect people’s height. The work also uncovers previously unrecognized biological mechanisms that underly human growth.

The findings, published on 25 November in Nature1, might help with the development of treatments that mitigate height changes caused by some medical conditions, such as forms of dwarfism.

“The impact these genes have on any given individual can be massive in terms of accurately predicting their height or making sure they’re getting the right treatment for a disease,” says Adam Locke, a statistical geneticist at the Regeneron Genetics Center in Tarrytown, New York.

About 80–90% of variation in adult height is caused by genetics. Projects analysing common gene variants have mapped thousands of DNA changes that can influence height. For example, a 2022 study identified more than 12,000 common genetic variants that collectively accounted for 40% of height variation in populations with European ancestry2.

However, how rare genetic variants (those found in less than 1% of a population) affect people’s height is less well studied.

To systematically probe how rare variants contribute to people’s stature, Locke and his colleagues gathered DNA and height data. In total, they looked at sequencing data from more than 1.4 million adults. They analysed the protein-coding sections of DNA and ran a series of tests to spot non-random links between height and both common and rare gene variants.

The analysis uncovered rare variants in 207 genes, which, on average, were linked to a height difference of about two centimetres. The team also identified 17 genes that had a particularly strong effect on height. The variants associated with this gene set all resulted in the production of non-functional proteins. In the study, over 700 people had at least one of these loss-of-function variants.

Genetic study homes in on height’s heritability mystery

Genetic study homes in on height’s heritability mystery

Individuals carrying such a variant were, on average, about nine centimetres taller or shorter than were people who didn’t have that variant. The strongest effects included a 17-centimetre reduction in height associated with a change to the ACAN gene and an 11-centimetre increase linked to the FBN1 gene. These effect sizes are more than 50 times larger than those of most genes commonly associated with height.

“We would expect rare genetic variants that disrupt gene function to have larger effects than common genetic variants, but the magnitude of some of these effects is particularly striking,” says Andrew Wood, a statistical geneticist at the University of Exeter, UK.

#1190. Lee Carsley Confirms his Stance on Tottenham and England U21 Star Archie Gray

England U21s manager Lee Carsley shared his thoughts on Archie Gray with GIVEMESPORT, as the Tottenham midfielder approaches a vital decision about his international career.

Carsley has been busy preparing for next summer's European Championship, as he looks to secure silverware for the third time in charge of the U21s.

The task ahead has now become even clearer following the official draw. The young Three Lions will square off against France, Poland and co-hosts Serbia in Group A in what Carsley hopes will hand his side a routine entry into the knockout stage.

Just who will be involved in Carsley's squad is now the big question. European football is scattered with top English talents these days and the U21s boss is expected to take full advantage of that.

Carsley spoke to GIVEMESPORT following the draw in Belgrade on Thursday, having his say on several young stars in the process.

The 52-year-old took the opportunity to speak about the likes of Manchester United youngster Ayden Heaven, as well as Gray, who has a particularly important decision to make in the near future.

The versatile Tottenham star has represented England from U15 to U21 level, but is yet to receive a senior call-up. As long as that is the case, the rules dictate that he will be allowed to represent another national team at senior level as long as he is eligible.

England's 20 best players right now have been ranked, including Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham and Bukayo Saka.

That should offer Scotland some hope. Gray is eligible to play for England's rivals through his father, Andy Gray, who made two appearances for Scotland, his grandfather Frank Gray, who was a European champion with Nottingham Forest and became a star defender with Scotland, and great-uncle Eddie Gray, who also played in front of the Tartan Army.

It's certainly a predicament for the 20-year-old, but he's already had a conversation about his potential England future with Carsley.

"Archie, like a lot of the players, is important to the Under-21s. He’s got a fantastic history in the pathway, a player that we really enjoy working with. There’s no change to what we spoke about previously."

The England U21s boss kept his cards close to his chest when it came to the details of that conversation, but Gray is certainly someone that he rates.

Whether Thomas Tuchel feels the same way remains to be seen. If the Three Lions are to turn the Spurs man into a fully-fledged England international, then they may have to do so sooner rather than later.

It's not just Carsley who's had his say on Gray's international career. The midfielder, himself, has also commented. He admitted back in 2024 that his desire is to represent England in a major blow for Scotland.

He told reporters: "My hopes are to play for England, definitely. It’s where I’m from and where I’ve grown up. I’m three quarters English, so that’s where’ I’m at. My dad is totally happy for whatever makes me happy, even though Eddie supports Scotland. But I’m the same as him, I’m happy as long as he’s happy.

"Hopefully I can (get England recognition), but I’ve just got to take it step by step and keep focusing on my club football, which can hopefully attract the attention of whoever it is, whether it’s the Under-21s or it’s the first team. I’d be really happy just to play for my country."

Whether that lasts the test of time if Gray fails to earn a senior England call-up is the big unanswered question, however. He certainly wouldn't be the first player to switch allegiances.

#1189. Arsenal's tifo for crunch clash with Man City will NOT mention Premier League guilty verdict as insiders lift lid on plans for new design ahead of Emirates contest

Published: 16:30 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 10:13 EST, 27 November 2026

Tifos are back at the Emirates. Those loud, passionate designs which last season galvanised Arsenal en route to a first Premier League title in 22 years return on Sunday for the visit of Manchester City.

An emotionally-charged fixture between the title holders and the team found guilty of the majority of 115 breaches of the league's financial rules by an independent commission (which is being appealed by Man City) awaits.

Still, it can be revealed that Sunday's display will be more restrained than initially considered.

Daily Mail Sport understands that a supporter-led group, established by the Arsenal Advisory Board (AAB) last season, initially raised an idea with Arsenal of referencing Man City's charges in the tifo. However, following consultation with the club, collectively the idea was dropped.

Instead the tifo will be done 'in the Arsenal way to inspire the fanbase', a source says. They added: 'It will galvanise and charge the fans in the right way.'

These matters can often be delicate. For example, it's understood a debate was had over the north London derby tifo ahead of Arsenal vs Tottenham in November 2025 at the Emirates, which involved a montage of club icons from past and present. And at the very top, positioned deliberately, sat Sol Campbell.

Sol Campbell, perched atop this Arsenal tifo for the derby game against Tottenham last season, moved between the clubs in a highly contentious transfer in 2001

What Arsenal offered on that PSG night in 2025 caused embarrassment – a solitary white cannon on a red backdrop

His 2001 move from Spurs to the Gunners remains one of the rivalry's deepest fault lines. Arsenal initially thought it could be too provocative but proceeded as the group were adamant on the imagery.

The reception when the tifo unveiled was immediate. The players felt it. The supporters felt it. Thierry Henry himself shared the image on social media with a simple verdict: 'What a tifo! Thank you, Gooners!'

As revealed in the book 22 Years: The Inside Story of Arsenal's Title-Winning Season, later in the season Mikel Arteta met up with the creators to say thank you and gifted each of them a signed, framed picture of the Tottenham tifo. Stuart MacFarlane, the club's chief photographer, was also there to take pictures of the group alongside Arteta. The Spaniard privately values the energy these displays create and embraces them.

It's understood Arteta checks the tifo designs before they are finalised. Much work goes into creating them, as reflected in the final proposal for Sunday's tifo which had to be confirmed and sent to the manufacturers nearly three weeks before matchday.

The artwork is printed on a square shape canvas which is then cut out and backed onto a paper-like material. That is cable-tied to a huge rectangular netting and tied to the roof with further cables and ropes.

The design along with the attached apparatus weighs around a couple of hundred kilograms, which is a serious amount. The lightweight fabric also has to be fire retardant and meet weight restrictions.

The work involved in putting the tifo together has seen volunteers invited to the Hale End academy this Friday to cable tie the tifo and get the design laid out on an indoor pitch.

Budgets have to be met, too, for the group are allocated an undisclosed amount to cover tifos for the whole season. Blowing the budget on one or two displays would rule out further spectacles later in the season.

The latest design builds on a growing trend which Arsenal began to grasp just over a year ago, the mission to properly create tifos initially starting in April 2025. Arsenal had unveiled their own tifo ahead of a Champions League semi-final first leg against Paris Saint-Germain — the first to be draped from the Emirates Stadium's roof in the arena's history.

For those confused by the term 'tifo', it stems from the Italian word tifosi, meaning passionate supporters. The designs are an attempt to galvanise fans, building an atmosphere with powerful messaging and provocative imagery to unsettle opponents.

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta checks the tifo designs before they are unveiled

Mikel Arteta said he hopes Manchester City's guilty verdict for breaching Premier League financial rules does not overshadow Sunday's crunch clash against Arsenal.

Man City were found guilty of the large majority of charges for breaking the league's financial regulations between 2009 and 2018, in a period which saw them win eight trophies. The Manchester club insist they're innocent and are appealing the independent commission's verdict.

When asked about whether the charges will overshadow the match, Arteta said: 'I hope that it doesn't because it's a process that is still open, it's not resolved and I don't know what is going to happen.

'I think when we have two teams at the level that they both are at right now with the quality players that are on that pitch, it's a massive game and a big game to enjoy.'

He added: 'That (the match) is the only thing that we should put the energy and the focus in. There's nothing else.'

Meanwhile, Arteta said there is a chance David Raya will be fit enough to play on Sunday.

Raya appeared to be in agony as he was forced off in the 70th minute of Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Newcastle last Saturday, hurting his left shoulder in an accidental collision with William Osula.

There were initial fears the goalkeeper could be facing an extended spell on the sidelines, with Kepa Arrizabalaga playing in Tuesday's Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund.

Arteta said: 'We still have a few hours before the game. We're still trying to get everyone back.'

On if there's 'a ray of hope' that Raya will be available, he added: 'Yeah.'

What Arsenal offered on that PSG night was widely mocked – a solitary white cannon on a red backdrop. That was it. A sterile design for one of the biggest European nights the Emirates had ever hosted, at that time.

It's understood a club-produced design had been used over a fan-led alternative, mainly because there was limited time between the proposal and the game itself.

The episode proved to be a pivotal turning point, led by the AAB.

The AAB is the club's formal fan-engagement body, created in 2021 following the backlash over Arsenal's involvement in the wretched European Super League plot — a breakaway competition set to feature 12 of Europe's leading clubs. The subsequent supporter anger forced Arsenal to improve their communication with fans.

After the PSG tifo disappointment, the AAB helped create a new group for the start of the 2025–26 season focused on creating tifos. Arsenal wanted to learn from the error, and this was their way of putting fans back in control.

It's worked. The outcome resulted in a slew of eye-catching displays in the previous campaign from Campbell to Leandro Trossard's eye-goggles celebration for the 'history in our sights' tifo ahead of the Champions League quarter-final second leg against Sporting Lisbon — or the 'over land and sea' design with a huge ship for the semi-final second leg against Atletico Madrid.

By softening the parameters and letting fan representatives into the inner sanctum, Arsenal have utilised a marginal gain Arteta had craved ever since he took charge seven years ago — make the Emirates a fortress.

While there was an initial temptation from the AAB to reference Man City's guilty verdict in Sunday's tifo, the overall message will be unmistakably clear: Arsenal are now in charge.

#1188. Trafford shows he has credentials to dislodge Pickford as England No 1

Has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

This was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

The first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

That result means that Sunderland’s stay bottom of the Premier League and without a win in the competition since August 30, while Leeds earn their fifth draw in eight top-flight fixtures to move up to seventh on 11 points.

We go into every game confident and ready to fight for the three points. We are here to win. We are going for every game [because] we want to win so we will try our best and fight.

Right now, I think his intensity against the ball, his workload against the ball, is on a way better level in comparison to how it was when he arrived and as soon as he adapts, I’m pretty sure his quality will shine through sooner rather than later.

Leeds are always a good side, it was in the Championship and now in the Premier League.

They are doing really well, they are consistent as well. They built momentum early in the season, which is always good, so they are in a different position but anything is possible in football. We think that it is going to be a new opportunity to get better.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

The return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a big boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Sunderland: Roefs, Hume, Mukiele, O’Nien, Reinildo, Xhaka, Sadiki, Le Fée, Rigg, Angulo, BrobbeySubs: Ellborg, Methalie, Alderete, Diarra, Ahoka, Talbi, Fofana, Angulo, Tuterov

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

Following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland currently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

Meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”

Lorenzo Bettoni is joined by Empire of the Kop editor Farrell Keeling to discuss the latest developments involving two Italy internationals with strong Liverpool connections: Giovanni Leoni and Federico Chiesa.

The conversation provides an update on Leoni’s recovery and expected return to action, while also assessing Chiesa’s situation at Anfield and what the future may hold for the former Juventus and Fiorentina star.

#1186. Adžić undergoes surgery as Juventus loanee’s Sassuolo season may be over

Vasilije Adžić has undergone knee surgery, and the Juventus loanee could miss the rest of the season with Sassuolo.

According to a statement from Juventus, the 20-year-old Montenegro international suffered a sprain and bruising to his right knee in Montenegro’s Nations League game against Cyprus on 15 November. Tests revealed “a small osteochondral detachment”, meaning a piece of bone and cartilage had come away inside the joint.

Adžić had surgery on Thursday at the Hôpital Privé Jean Mermoz in Lyon, where Juventus captain Manuel Locatelli was also operated on in September. He has now started the rehabilitation programme “aimed at returning to competitive activity”.

Neither Juventus nor Sassuolo have given a timeframe for his recovery. However, TuttoMercatoWeb suggests the need for surgery points to a lengthy absence, with a real risk he won’t play again before the end of the 2026-27 season.

It’s a cruel blow for a player who started his loan in style. Adžić scored in three consecutive Serie A games in September, including a curling winner off the bench in Sassuolo’s 3-2 victory over Juventus. His form has tailed off since then, and he has three goals and one assist in nine league appearances.

The injury could also affect his future. Sassuolo paid €500,000 to take him on loan in the summer and included an option to buy fixed at €12m, while Juventus kept a buy-back clause. A long spell out leaves both clubs with little to go on when they decide his future next summer.

#1185. Succumbing to certainty is a failure in science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Scientists should resist political pressure to provide certainty when the evidence suggests otherwise, says Andy Stirling.Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Science’s greatest failure is not getting things wrong, but by sometimes pretending that there is more certainty than there really is, says social scientist Andy Stirling.

This can happen, he says, when researchers face political pressure to provide a single, definitive answer, when the evidence is far more complex.

In the final episode of a six-part podcast series about failure in science, Stirling, an emeritus professor at the University of Sussex in Brighton, UK, draws on examples from climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic, environmental campaigns and energy policy.

“In those areas, science just does not convey the degree of uncertainty and of variability and of how many potentially viable options are being cut out when you just give one clear answer,” he says. “It thinks it’s helping society by just giving one picture of the truth. And in fact, it’s undermining both itself and democracy when it does that.”

Stirling, whose research includes science and technology policy and environmental politics, says that on occasions politicians have almost literally hidden behind scientists on a podium, who have relied on their authority and expertise to protect them.

Earlier this year, Stirling spoke at a one-day conference on failure in science, with a focus on careers and innovation. It was held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03837-y

Well, my failure is to take my own advice.

The thing I want to say here, I, you know, talk the talk.

I’m big on talking the talk, but walking the walk is tricky.

That’s social scientist Professor Andy Stirling at the opening session of the Failure in Science conference, held at Imperial College London in April 2026.

It’s why I’m so motivated. I’ll create a false frisson of expectation.

It’s why I’m so motivated to say what I’m going to say in this panel that it is so difficult.

Up until now, in this series, we’ve talked about individual scientists seeing failure come their way.

And we’ve talked about science institutions, universities, trying to get good at allowing failure as part and parcel of science.

But as a social scientist peering at science through that lens, Professor Stirling takes this a step further.

I’m trying to contribute with many others to a move towards making it okay to speak about how the results we get in science are never, even when we are massively successful, never mind when we’re failing.

They are never as singular, and unambiguous, and definitive as our disciplines, our superiors, and policymakers force us to pretend.

If science is supposed to exist for the betterment of humanity, is it actually doing a good job?

Does science fail sometimes or often when it heads out into society?

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

In episode six, we explore how the very project of science sometimes fails our society, and we discuss how it could adapt to better serve its citizens.

We’re asking, how can good science and good science policy benefit from admitting that sometimes we don’t really know?

What we’re discussing here, of course, is science and democracy, where we like to believe everyone has their say.

Well, my name’s Andy Stirling, and I’m a professor at the University of Sussex, and visiting or honorary at UCL and Leiden.

Given that my topic is on how science functions in society, one of my best candidates, I think, for a failure is just being so slow to realize how power works around science.

I’ve spent years, you know, chipping in in modest ways on advisory processes, advisory committees on this and that topic because of the nature of the work I do, and it took me a long time to realize just how powerful the forces are that pressurize science into giving certain kinds of answers, or not asking certain kinds of questions.

Those forces are much more powerful than I had thought at the beginning. Even though I thought of myself quite hard-nosed, I’ve really been quite surprised.

Sure, yeah. Well, look, it was a fantastic conference all around different aspects of failure, and that was in the context of a lot of people talking really eloquently about failure within science, and actually how science can benefit and people can benefit from failure.

So that was a context for me picking up that science itself has, in an important sense, failed itself and society.

And in saying that, I absolutely didn’t say it out of a spirit of being critical of science.

It’s because I am so enthusiastic. I regard science as so precious that the disappointment, as it were, of that is all the more acute when you value science in society.

And I said it because, in a nutshell, I think science fails to communicate the most important thing about itself to society, and that matters because the times in which people are most listening to science is when there’s some kind of crisis about climate, about some sort of technology that’s causing a risk, about what to do with future innovation.

So on those areas, science just does not convey the degree of uncertainty and of variability and of how many potentially viable options are being cut out when you just give one clear answer.

It thinks it’s helping society by just giving one picture of the truth.

And in fact, it’s undermining both itself and democracy when it does that.

You’ll probably want to unpack what I mean by all that, but that’s the nutshell.

So yeah, I think it is useful to see science as a social movement. That’s not the only way to see it. There’s all kinds of different views. It’s in the spirit of my, what I’m trying to say that there are different ways of viewing this one thing.

But all the more important because it gets neglected.

Science is very often as much by critics sometimes as by its protagonists, put forward in any given area as being some objective source of authority, a definitive authority.

And even if uncertainties are acknowledged, there’s a kind of disembodied, detached idea of scientific expertise.

And one can understand that. I mean, I say this in the spirit of really respecting how amazing the transcendent kind of progress can be in areas by really applying scientific method.

But we tend to forget that science is itself located in society.

So the kinds of questions that it asks, the kinds of resources that are applied, the kinds of attitudes that it takes when it’s challenged or when it’s trying to influence, is very human, subject to all kinds of interest.

I mean, how often do scientists display enormous enthusiasm about their particular field, often their particular technology?

They’re highly partisan. It comes with the ability to be highly critical. It doesn’t, it’s not separate.

There’s certain questions won’t be asked for many years unless you get different disciplines together, and then they’ll ask each other more difficult questions. But often they won’t even talk to each other.

So yeah, it’s a social movement. It’s a collection of social movements, and by that I mean, I mean it’s got all kinds of institutions and organizations and cultures in it.

But maybe a good way to illustrate this is the Royal Society, one of the first in the modern idea of science in the world.

Their motto in the 17th century was nullius in verba. Not on anyone’s word, not on authority.

And it is deliciously ironic when you see now these enormous reports on nuclear or geoengineering or gene editing being slapped down on the table with the motto nullius in verba, when in fact it is being used as a source of authority.

But the the foundation of science, it was a reaction to doctrinal assertions from the monarchy or from the church.

And scientists were saying we want to argue about it. We want to have experiments. We want to have analysis. We want to have reasoned arguments about how you can draw different conclusions.

And of course, in the beginning, that was highly exclusive. It was old white males.

But nonetheless, the principle was you should be able to argue with each other, irrespective of your authority.

And now, I’m afraid, science is often a little bit seduced by power and privilege. It gets locked into patronage networks so that, you know, it gets rewarded, and too often it sees itself as a source of authority rather than a source of questions.

When we say with climate change, what does the, what does, do what the science says.

There are a lot of activists come out with banners saying that, but also you know chief scientists often find themselves saying something similar.

And you can’t because the science says nothing without values and interests to help frame it.

There’s nothing about evidence and data in the climate area as anywhere else that actually compels you to act in a particular way.

It’s really crucial. I say this as somebody who’s worked on climate since the 80s, but it’s not the science that tells us what to do.

It’s also the science, along with values and interests and experience, that helps us shape and frame the science that really matters.

And why that matters is we basically block the politics out. And we block out that you can get different answers from the same data by asking the question differently or different questions.

And if we block that out, what we’re doing is being authoritarian, because we’re just giving one answer.

We’re hiding the values that give you that one answer, and then for those people who don’t share those values, by doing that, we’re being authoritarian. And instead of prompting compliance, we provoke a backlash, an authoritarian backlash.

So when science laments the post-truth authoritarianism that it experiences in many areas, it’s I think to a large extent seeing itself in the mirror.

And if it was more honest about its own uncertainties, its own politics, the way there’s always different answers you could get from any given model, we might get a more reasoned debate.

If you think back to the history of environmentalism and ask when was it most successful, you know everyone will have different views of this.

It’s in the spirit of my analysis that there’s different stories to be told.

But whether it’s whales, pesticides, chlorine chemicals, heavy metals. Although none of these issues have finally been won, there were some major victories took place in the history of environmentalism, rightly or wrongly, in which things were withdrawn from.

And across the board, the way that was done was against science, quite often expert scientists, academics, industry, government, universities, saying, "Look, we’ve done the science. It’s okay. We’ve done the calculations. We have models of the dispersion in the ocean."

And the environmentalists said, "We don’t believe your science. We think it’s been shaped by the kinds of power around it.

"And we’re talking about values. It’s just wrong to do this. And if you look at your model in a different way, you’ll get a different answer. You’ll get the answer we get."

And then again and again and again, environmentalists won on that kind of argument. By the time you roll around as as science and also especially environmentalism become institutionalized, you get exactly the arguments that lost being deployed in favour of climate change.

We’ve done the models. We’re global. We’ve modeled the entire global climate system. We thought up something called global mean temperature.

We are insisting it should be static, when in fact we know it’s dynamic, and we’re defining it to very high degrees of precision and saying our models will be the means by which the world addresses this problem.

So rather than doing it in terms of virtues and values and the kind of society we want to live in, which lost in the past.

We’re doing it on do what the science says, which lost in the past, arguably rightly, because you can’t do what the science says, and in the process we’re provoking exactly the backlash, as I mentioned earlier.

So that’s an example of the kinds of ways it’s been lost. That climate is of absolutely crucial importance, but it should be recognized to be a struggle, a democratic struggle, and not just based on science, because that’s the way you actually lose issues, not win them.

To behave like that is itself post-truth.

When science downplays its uncertainties, downplays the sensitivities, the way in which different assumptions in the model, which are equally reasonable, could get a different answer, the way in which values, emotions, virtues, ideologies all play a role in science, just like they do outside.

When it pretends that’s not the case, it is in fact behaving in a post-truth way, and so then it’s not surprising it gets a post-truth reaction.

So doubling down on that is exactly...it’s like throwing kerosene on the fire. It’s just not going to work to. Your self behaving in this authoritarian way and expect other authoritarianisms to go away.

We should be informing democracy and achieving these changes through democratic struggle. And science is absolutely essential to that, but only if it conducts itself in an honest way.

One thing that got me going with all this was in back in the ’90 s I was looking at risk assessments, cost-benefit analysis, life cycle assessments.

All these highly technical quantitative assessments in the energy sector.

Cutting a long story short, they were, the energy sector was the place where these things were developed to their most mature, sophisticated form. And if you looked at any given study, you got this really confident idea.

This is what the risks of nuclear are compared to renewables, compared to gas, or whatever it is.

The same with the other methods I mentioned.

And then every single time you stand back and you look at the literature as a whole, not just peer-reviewed literature, but the literature embodied in law.

So the most kind of authoritatively treated source of data on these things, and you found you could get any answer you like across that peer-reviewed literature.

It depends on the framing. The models give you an answer that depends on how you frame the question.

And that for me kind of radicalized me because I realized that none of the committees, none of the reports around the world were fully representing what the literature they were consulting told us, that you can get all kinds of different answers.

And what matters is not just the one answer, the risk, the cost, environmental costs, the ecosystem service.

What matters is how that changes depending on assumptions, that’s how science should speak to policy, but also to society, telling us how these things depend.

The reason I said that, a lot of people talk about lamenting the fact we have policy-based evidence rather than evidence-based policy, and it’s a good point.

You know, you get all kinds of practices making things up all the time, all over the place in every sector.

But my point wasn’t to lambast that. It wasn’t to say, to lament yet again "you guys are just stitching it up." It was to say "Actually, I’ve never yet seen an area where the evidence compels a single policy."

So even when you do get the best quality evidence, it is never without uncertainties. It’s never without differences of implication for action, depending on which discipline was actually most influential, how the questions were asked, what the baselines were, etc. etc.

So I have yet to see any body of analysis based on evidence that compels a single decision.

So when you hear people talking about evidence-based policy as if there were only one policy that could have been based on the evidence, they’re basically again being post-truth.

They’re (to be a bit more colourful about it, they’re telling porkies."

Because there will always be values, interests, assumptions at work, and it’s not a bad thing. It’s inevitable.

That’s how science, you know, depends. For instance, on BSE whether vets or were the epidemiologists in charge? He got a very different answer.

And in COVID, you know, again, we-I mean, it’s still too early to say, as Mao said, I think about the French Revolution, was it? But it’s too early to say.

But you can still see that what was the best way to act on the available evidence, economic as well as epidemiological, and the different ways of interpreting the epidemiological evidence.

It’s very clear now that it’s not so clear-cut what a particular country should do.

Different countries do different things. There are different ways of looking back on it, looking at the time and seeing what was good and what was bad.

So, without taking position on either side, it’s far from clear that there was a single definitive action that should have been taken.

I defy anyone to actually come back and defend that. There’ll be a matter of judgment as between really quite radically different policies.

So COVID is an example of this. I think we had to pretend there was one policy because it was so stressful.

Politicians had to pretend because otherwise they would have to hide behind their chief scientists, literally sometimes, literally behind them on the podium, hiding behind them because they needed that authority to protect them from the inevitable uncertainties that everyone believed were really there, even though they weren’t acknowledging it in the graphs.

I mean, blame management, trust, public acceptance.

These things are the most important commodities in politics. So yeah, and it’s you know apocryphally, people have all kinds of anecdotes out on these advisory committees.

I’ve served a little bit on some of them. You know, the number of times in which the politicians will intimate, "I won’t hesitate to hide behind you," almost as a joke.

But so you know, scientists respond to that in different ways. But by and large, they think, "Well, okay, we’ve got to be responsible. Let’s give these guys a single prescriptive answer, even though we know among ourselves that we could have got a different answer, but we’ve got a responsibility not to do an to do to do an elevator pitch."

You know, not to give on the one hand, on the other, as Margaret Thatcher said, "Save me from the two-handed economist. I want a one-handed economist."

She wants it because of justification, but actually, it’s a responsibility of the economist, or in this case, a scientist, to actually explain how it does depend. It always does depend.

If they don’t explain that, then they are failing, I would say science, and failing society, failing democracy.

Other things are really complicated. there’s a lot of real challenges. I don’t want to pretend it’s easier than it really is.

But actually, we shouldn’t be paralyzed by this. Look at science itself. When it developed in the 17th century, motto of the Royal Society, nullius in verba, that was basically saying that principles of accountability, of argument, of deliberation really mattered, of treating people more equally than many institutions do. That’s not the opposite of democracy. That is democracy.

Science was about, in many ways, democratizing knowledge.

You know, you needed to argue, you need to show evidence and do analyzes in rigorous ways. But it should be open to anyone to do that, and to any perspective, no matter how ridiculous it sounds, if it can substantiate itself.

So science and democracy are not on opposite sides.

So I think, rather than counterpointing them, like science is against democracy, we can’t trust democracy, going to undermine science, actually, see it the other way round: that science is an embodiment of democracy.

It’s when it is at its best. It’s when it’s being democratic about the ability to challenge power inside science, and that’s how we solve the problems of science.

It’s also how we solve the problems at the moment of democracy, which science is, sadly, because it’s forced to be more authoritarian in pretending a singular truth.

It’s forced into that not by democracy, but by power that is also eroding democracy.

Science, when it comes to advise policymakers, yes, please do your best, but don’t think of yourself just giving a single expedient answer so that a politician goes away happy and can act without worrying about blame.

Inform society at large about the assumptions that went into that.

Show how it depends, and if you do that, you’re informing democracy as much as the powerful actors who are, you know, maybe conferring the patronage on the scientists.

Science fails when it’s not being plural enough.

It needs to be plural about who’s involved, about the questions that are asked, about the disciplines that get around the table, about how it conveys its interpretations of its understandings out to society, and it needs to just not be scared of representing that plurality because with that comes the conditions.

It’s not just anything goes. It’s not plural for plurality’s sake.

It’s then saying under what conditions you get answer X or answer Y, and that’s more scientific.

It’s more rigorous to behave in that way.

When science does that, it’s being more scientific when it’s plural. So I think science fails most when it reduces all those kinds of plurality.

#1184. How Leeds United turned into Champions League contenders: Insiders reveal the ways 'manager's dream' Ethan Ampadu drives standards on and off the pitch, a hidden tougher side to Daniel Farke - and the club's January transfer window strategy

Published: 07:04 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 10:46 EST, 27 November 2026

He may not realise it yet, but the key member of Leeds United’s ever-improving team might just become one of their next great managers.

Leeds have been deservedly praised for their impressive start to the season, which sees them a point away from the likely Champions League places ahead of Saturday’s clash with Coventry.

Boss Daniel Farke is re-establishing the club in the top flight. Dominic Calvert-Lewin has signed a new contract and is an England player again. Towering centre back Tarik Muharemovic looks the buy of the season. The 49ers Enterprises Group are shrewd and careful owners.

But what about the guy who knits it all together? Ethan Ampadu had played for six clubs in three countries before he joined Leeds in 2023 but now he has found his home. Nearly half of Ampadu’s senior appearances have been in a Leeds shirt.

Ampadu’s work on the pitch and his behaviour off it suggest a manager in the making. Team-mates turn to him instinctively during matches and off the field, too, he makes Leeds tick.

‘I don’t know what Ethan’s plans are when he's finished playing but he has the stature and could offer a lot to the game beyond his playing career,’ says Stuart Dallas, who helped Leeds return to the Premier League in 2020 during an outstanding nine-year career at Elland Road.

Here Daily Mail Sport looks at why Leeds are on the rise – starting with their inspirational captain.

Inspired by brilliant new signings including Tarik Muharemovic (left) and James Trafford, Leeds are on the rise and in contention for the Champions League spots

Captain Ethan Ampadu makes Leeds tick on and off the pitch and is perceived as a manager in waiting

In the here and now, boss Daniel Farke is doing a superb job, having narrowly avoided being sacked in previous seasons

Though Dallas retired due to injury at the end of Ampadu’s first campaign at Leeds, he liked what he saw in those months.

‘I was at the training ground recently and the players had a later start – they were preparing for a Sunday game,’ Dallas, now a regular television pundit, tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘He was the first to turn up for the session. If you’re a young player coming through, it’s fantastic to see the captain setting that example.

‘He is an intelligent guy who takes responsibility. In his position you have to front up when things are not going well and protect people when they need it. He understands that.

‘A manager doesn’t want 20 different people knocking on his door. Ethan will take a lot of those minor problems away and I know how much of a privilege it is to him to captain Leeds.’

Ampadu takes the role extremely seriously. Daily Mail Sport understands he ensured Under-21 players who train regularly with the first team were included in the players' bonus pool. He also made sure they were listed as first-team squad members on the club website.

Ampadu wants the squad to feel like a family and will organise team bonding trips and meals out. Little things like that go a heck of a long way.

The club's leadership group comprises Ampadu, Calvert-Lewin, Jaka Bijol, Joe Rodon and James Justin – but third-choice goalkeeper Alex Cairns is another hugely respected figure in the squad.

Prolific striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin (pictured scoring in Leeds' 4-1 rout of Chelsea last weekend) has signed a new contract with the club

Calvert-Lewin (with Noah Okafor, right) is part of the team's leadership group, led by Ampadu

‘Ethan is a manager’s dream,’ explains former Leeds boss Simon Grayson, now a regular pundit on Leeds’ in-house TV channel LUTV. ‘Someone like that makes the manager’s job much less stressful.

‘If there’s an incident on or off the pitch, sometimes the captain can deal with it before it reaches the manager’s door. Ethan will do that. He has a level of respect from the other players so if he says something, it’s no different from Daniel Farke saying it.’

Farke is usually cautious when bringing back players from injury. When they are as important as Ampadu, though, he is prepared to make an exception.

The 26-year-old does not immediately catch the eye. He does not make spectacular passes or beat three opponents with a piece of skill. He has only three goals in 139 appearances.

Instead, he steps back into defence to cover the forward runs of Justin or Jayden Bogle. He makes sure he is in the right spot to stop counter-attacks. He is the one to notice when a team-mate has drifted out of position when defending a set-piece. Scouts see this and this is why Ampadu was considered by clubs in the so-called ‘Big Six’ before he signed a new four-year deal with Leeds last June.

‘He’ll go in and smash someone – fairly – if it’s a quiet game because it will wake the crowd up a bit,’ smiles Grayson. ‘You only realise how much you miss players like that when they are not in the team.’

Ampadu is just as popular with the fans. ‘As Leeds captains go, Gary McAllister and Lucas Radebe set a high bar when I was growing up,' says Rocco Dean of the Leeds, That! podcast. 'Although Ampadu has a little way to go, it's not inconceivable he could one day rank alongside those greats.'

At any time, there will usually be two or three players in a squad who are not popular with supporters. It is difficult to find them in the current Leeds side. ‘The players want to play for Leeds and it’s not just a "job",’ adds Mike Chard, who runs the All Leeds TV YouTube channel. ‘They don’t seem like a team. They seem like a family.’

‘As Leeds captains go, Gary McAllister and Lucas Radebe set a high bar when I was growing up... but Ampadu could one day rank alongside those greats'

Leeds have a broad agreement with Farke over a new contract and he deserves it. If Leeds beat Coventry, it will be his 80th win as boss in 162 games. Bielsa reached 80 in 163 matches.

In front of the cameras, Farke is open and affable – but he is no soft touch with his squad or coaches. The staff member who wore a snood over his head to training this week will be forced to don shorts and T-shirt for the remainder of the winter. His crime? Acting ‘big time’.

Footballers like to fool about when they are together but few would dare risk it when Farke is nearby. Daily Mail Sport has heard of one player who was acting the goat in the canteen and turned white when he realised he had failed to notice Farke entering the room.

Some bosses will encourage players to ask why they have been left out of the team. That is not typically the case with Farke. Generally, he makes his choices and then it falls to players to prove him wrong through their displays in training.

He can still forge close relationships with players, though. His rapport with Calvert-Lewin was a factor in the striker’s new deal and he has a similarly strong understanding with Noah Okafor.

Farke is probably as powerful now as he has ever been during his three-and-a-half seasons at Elland Road. At different points during his two Championship campaigns in charge, Farke was vulnerable to the sack. Even early last season, things looked a little dicey for him.

Switching to a back three in the 3-2 defeat at Manchester City last November turned it around for Leeds but this is about much more than a simple change of formation.

Despite his affable exterior and close bonds with certain players, Farke has a disciplinarian streak

Most of Leeds’ medical and conditioning team have been at Elland Road for more than a decade and unlike at many clubs, there is complete trust between them and Farke. The result? No injuries to first-team players as things stand.

On their instruction, Farke restricted Okafor to a 20-minute substitute appearance against Tottenham earlier this month. The Swiss attacker still scored the only goal.

In a typical week after a Saturday game, players will report to Thorp Arch for a recovery session on Sunday and have Monday off. Wednesday is usually the toughest day – gym in the morning followed by a training session, and more gym work in the afternoon.

Farke and his staff favour two particular possession drills: a four-a-side game with three ‘floating’ players who work with whoever has the ball, and a 10-a-side exercise with two floating players.

Brighton and Brentford have set the standard for recruitment in the last decade yet since promotion Leeds have not been far behind. Chairman Paraag Marathe has worked for global management consultants Bain, who rely heavily on data.

Led by sporting director Adam Underwood, Leeds do the same – though they mix art with science. New signings are shown videos of the celebrations in the city when Leeds were promoted in 2025. The current brief is to find physically robust, athletic players and unlike many clubs, Leeds are not obsessed with youth. The average age of their starting XI for the 4-1 win at Stamford Bridge was 27 years and 107 days. That figure has not dipped below 26 in any league game this season.

Underwood and his team anticipate a quiet January window in which no key players are expected to leave – dashing any hopes rivals may have had of stealing Muharemovic. The defender joined from Sassuolo for £30.1million last summer and his value is already much higher.

Under chairman Paraag Marathe (right), Leeds rely heavily on data in their recruitment. Their transfer track record has been excellent in recent years

The pinch point for the 49ers is coming. They aim to make Leeds worth £1billion by 2030. That will require significantly greater revenue: in 2024-25, when Leeds were promoted from the Championship, their revenue was £137m. That was a record for the second tier but they will likely need to exceed £300m in the coming years to hit the 49ers' £1bn target.

An expanded Elland Road should plug some of this gap when work is complete. Leeds are working on each stand in turn and hope the project will be finished by the end of 2030, giving them a 53,000 capacity.

Earlier this month, Leeds instructed US bank Allen & Co to seek additional investment, though it is thought a full sale is not currently on the cards.

Christian Purslow offers a different perspective. The former Aston Villa CEO, who also held senior positions at Liverpool and Chelsea, knows how tough it is for clubs outside the Big Six to break into that wealthy elite.

Speaking on The Football Boardcast, Purslow said: ‘If I were Paraag Marathe, I’d be looking at what’s gone on at some of my natural peers – Newcastle, Aston Villa, West Ham, Leicester, Everton. It’s so precarious when clubs like these try hard to push up against the so-called Big Six.

‘These guys (the 49ers) might conclude: "We’ve done our job, we’ve enjoyed the journey, let’s let someone else have the problem of competing with the Big Six in a world where Premier League and UEFA financial rules make it increasingly difficult." I would not rule that out in the next couple of years.’

‘They are allowed to dream big and enjoy themselves,’ Farke said of Leeds' supporters this week

Leeds are in no hurry. The sense at Elland Road is that the 49ers will not seek a shortcut by raising the wage bill or appointing a manager on a huge salary. They are prepared to go slow and steady.

As Purslow highlighted, if Newcastle – who have some of the world’s wealthiest owners – have accepted they cannot change the status quo, what chance does anyone else have?

After spending much of this century feeling gloomy, though, Leeds fans do not want to think about it too deeply.

‘They are allowed to dream big and enjoy themselves,’ Farke said this week. ‘After nearly three decades of suffering, it is a joy to bring this hope and belief back into the hearts, heads and souls of our supporters. This is why we are working so hard.’

#1183. What Bruno Fernandes’ new Manchester United contract means for Milan

Manchester United have triggered a one-year extension on Bruno Fernandes’ contract, ending Milan’s hopes of signing him on a free transfer next summer.

According to The Athletic, the club captain is now tied to Old Trafford until June 2028. Fernandes had been entering the final year of his deal and recently confirmed that talks over a new contract had been put on hold, with both sides wanting to focus on improving results.

By exercising the option, United have stopped the 32-year-old from negotiating with foreign clubs from 1 January, when he would otherwise have been free to agree a pre-contract.

That doesn’t rule out a move next year, but any club wanting Fernandes will now have to pay a fee. Milan are among the European clubs monitoring him, along with interest from Saudi Arabia, and United have already identified possible replacements.

The Portuguese midfielder’s future had looked uncertain after Michael Carrick dropped him for a 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth. That followed his public criticism of the team’s tactics after a 4-1 Champions League loss to Como.

Since then, however, Fernandes has kept the captaincy under new coach Mauricio Pochettino and scored twice in Wednesday’s 2-2 draw at Sporting CP.
