#1182. Europa Fight League! Marseille hooligans descend on Levski Sofia end after 'Nazi salute' - while Besiktas match is SUSPENDED due to pro-Palestine propaganda... and away fans infiltrate Sunderland

By LUKE POWER, SPORTS REPORTER and BOBBY MANZI, FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 16:06 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 12:19 EST, 27 November 2026

European football has endured another night of chaos with fan trouble at Marseille, Besiktas and Sunderland.

Marseille and Levski Sofia fans clashed violently at their Europa League match, with home hooligans descending on the away end with bats and metal pipes after being provoked by a Nazi salute.

Turkish side Besiktas' clash with Israeli team Hapoel Be'er Sheva was brought to a temporary halt after fans of the former unfurled a pro-Palestinian flag, leading to a clash with police.

And Sunderland's home end was infiltrated by supporters of Jagiellonia Bialystok, who had been banned for the fixture by UEFA - with some of the visitors starting brawls.

The three Europa League disturbances cast another dark shadow over football.

Marseille saw the worst events as an estimated 200-300 home hooligans entered the away end with bats, pipes, and flares.

Marseille's supporters descended on the Levski Sofia end with bats and flares

It is believed that the Marseille ultras were provoked by a Nazi salute by a Levski Sofia fan

One supporter at the Marseille-Levski Sofia match nursed a bleeding head injury

Besiktas fans unfurled a Palestine flag at their fixture against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er Sheva

They had reportedly been provoked by some of Levski's ultras, who have a long association with neo-Nazism, and Marseille's supporters responded with an antifascist chant.

In a statement released on Friday afternoon, UEFA said: 'We strongly condemn the serious incidents of violence and disorder, including the clashes involving supporters inside the stadium, that occurred in connection with the Europa League matches between Marseille and Levski Sofia as well as Besiktas and Hapoel Beer-Sheva.

'Violence, aggression, hatred and any form of provocative, discriminatory or extremist behaviour have no place in football. UEFA competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety.

'The events witnessed at the matches run counter to these fundamental values and to UEFA’s objective, enshrined in its statutes, of ensuring that football matches are played in a spirit of peace, mutual respect and sporting fairness.

'UEFA has appointed ethics and disciplinary inspectors to conduct investigations into the incidents and examine all available evidence to establish the relevant facts and circumstances in accordance with the applicable UEFA regulatory framework.'

Some people kicked and punched each other in Marseille - another even used a fire extinguisher, according to L'Equipe.

Bulgarian news agency Bgnes, meanwhile, reported that the French hooligans also hurled bottles, flares and firecrackers.

Women and members of Levski's entourage were among the crowd, and several injured supporters had to be escorted out of the stadium, according to reports.

'Olympique de Marseille condemns the incidents that occurred on the sidelines of the match against Levski Sofia,' the hosts said in a statement.

'The swift intervention of the club's security teams restored calm, without affecting the match itself.

'The club is currently working to establish the precise circumstances of these incidents, in conjunction with the relevant authorities.'

Elsewhere, trouble spiked in the 25th minute of Besiktas' 2-1 win over Hapoel Be'er Sheva.

One fan was seen being taken away on a stretcher at the Besiktas game, which was played in Batumi, Georgia

Besiktas full-back Kassoum Ouattara hung the Palestine flag over the advertising hoarding, covering the UEFA lettering

Police had to remove some Jagiellonia Bialystok fans who had infiltrated the home end at Sunderland

The match had been moved to Batumi, Georgia due to security worries surrounding ties between Turkish and Israeli clubs. There was even tension on the pitch, as Besiktas refused to shake hands with their opponents.

After a pro-Palestine banner was revealed by Besiktas' fans, the Georgian police appeared to react with tear gas or pepper spray and batons. One fan was seen being carried away on a stretcher.

The game had to be briefly suspended, with both sets of teams and the officials going to the dressing rooms.

After the match, Besiktas full-back Kassoum Ouattara hung the Palestine flag over the UEFA lettering on the pitchside advertising hoardings.

Besiktas condemned the local police, saying they had used 'disproportionate force'.

The club also wrote: 'Upon learning that security forces were obstructing our fans' entry into the stadium, we immediately contacted the UEFA delegate, who arranged for the stadium's evacuation gates to be opened, allowing our fans to enter the stadium quickly and safely.

'We announce that steps have been taken with our Consulate General in Batumi and UEFA regarding the disproportionate force used by security forces against our fans, and state that we will closely monitor the situation until each of our fans returns safely to our country.'

Turkey and Israel have long been simmering with tension amid the conflict and numerous Turkish clubs such as Galatasaray, Fenerbahce, and Mohamed Salah's Trabzonspor came out in support of Besiktas later - despite usually being bitter rivals.

A UEFA Disciplinary ruling meant Polish club Jagiellonia Białystok weren't meant to have any away supporters at The Stadium of Light for tonight's game at Sunderland, yet plenty of them have turned up in the home end… 🫣😭pic.twitter.com/lRBvHOp16T

Jagiellonia Bialystok's supporters had been banned - but some bought tickets in the home end

Meanwhile, at the Stadium of Light, events were of a lower scale, but some away fans were seen brawling with the home faithful and police waded in to eject them.

Jagiellonia Bialystok's fans had been banned from attending the game by UEFA following disturbances between them and Levski Sofia fans earlier this month.

But around 20 of them managed to secure tickets, Sunderland believe, and squeeze into the stadium.

The club had already caught some out in advance, writing: 'The club is actively monitoring ticket purchases and has identified and cancelled tickets purchased by, or on behalf of, individuals identified as Jagiellonia supporters.

'All affected tickets will be refunded to the original purchasers.

'This restriction applies across all areas of the stadium, including home sections, and regardless of how tickets have been purchased or transferred.

'Any attempt to circumvent the restriction, including using tickets purchased through third parties or belonging to other supporters, will result in refusal of entry.

'Jagiellonia supporters without a valid entitlement to attend the fixture are strongly advised not to travel to Sunderland.

'No Jagiellonia supporters without valid permission to attend will be permitted entry into the Stadium of Light, and we strongly advise they stay away from the immediate surrounding vicinity.

'The club will continue to work closely with the relevant authorities to ensure UEFA's ruling is fully enforced and that the fixture takes place as a home supporter-only event.'

#1181. Report: Lookman price tag set by Atletico as Roma monitor closely

Atlético Madrid are prepared to sell Ademola Lookman in January, less than a year after signing him from Atalanta.

According to Spanish outlet Fichajes, via CalcioMercato, the Nigerian forward is no longer considered untouchable by Diego Simeone, and the club would listen to offers. They won’t let him go cheaply, though. Atlético want a permanent sale worth at least the €35-40m they paid Atalanta last February.

Lookman is currently sidelined with a knee sprain picked up on international duty with Nigeria. The Super Eagles’ staff initially thought it was minor, but tests in Madrid showed a more serious problem, although the ligaments don’t appear to be involved. He is expected to be out until early 2027, which means he should return just as the January window opens.

Inter were previously strong admirers, but they now plan to spend their January budget on defence. That leaves Roma as the most likely Serie A destination.

Gian Piero Gasperini turned Lookman into one of Europe’s most dangerous forwards at Atalanta, despite their well-documented clashes over transfers. The Roma coach has been looking for a player with his profile since the summer.

Roma also have a good relationship with Atlético, having already done business with them over Nahuel Molina.

#1180. Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick

Hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

More than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

An announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

That is how far United have, once again, fallen. Fans in the Stretford End unfurled their “Standards” banner, bearing the faces of Eric Cantona, Roy Keane and Bryan Robson.

It was first revealed in December 2021 in Carrick’s final match as interim following Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s sacking. This should be his final game again, under different, more traumatic, circumstances.

If it is, he is going out having made a stand. He dropped Bruno Fernandes for his outspoken comments, aimed directly at Carrick and his tactics, following the dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat away to Como on Wednesday.

At 2-0 down here it was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha when he substituted Youri Tielemans, who had been so terribly slow and ineffective, at half-time. Carrick did not bring on Fernandes. And he did not turn to the captain after, as he made four substitutions, including bringing on 19-year-old Shea Lacey. That said it all.

The television cameras catching Omar Berrada, the United chief executive, shaking his head in the stands as Carrick’s team gave away goals also told its own story. They have two wins from 12 in all competitions and none in eight. They have only beaten newly promoted Ipswich Town, in August, and Azerbaijan minnows Sabah this season. United were so careless it looked like they could not care less.

There was no guarantee, after Como, that Carrick would remain in charge after this game. So, losing and losing so embarrassingly – it was three, it should have been five – has to have obvious consequences. However cherished Carrick is. However much the fans excuse him. Yes, he has not been helped enough, but he has also not been good enough.

Finishing third and qualifying for the Champions League last season has proved to be the kind of bounce a new manager can achieve, after the pressure was relieved by the sacking of Ruben Amorim, rather than something more sustainable. There was always the fear that Carrick, despite his playing pedigree, might be out of his depth in this job. And so it is proving to be. Especially as he has been hung out to dry. Carrick certainly appeared resigned to his fate.

But what is he coaching? What is he trying to do with United? How does he want his team to play? Yes, there are limitations, but they are badly set up, tactically poor, and struggle to build attacks. The players are not responding, but it does not mean Carrick is blameless.

Bournemouth were not just collectively and individually better – and despite how good they are, that is some indictment of United – but better organised. They knew what they were doing, believed in it and relished it as they collected a fourth victory, and a fourth clean sheet in a row, after a slow start under Marco Rose, the new head coach. It was no shock.

The nature of the goals spoke volumes. For the first, a free-kick was needlessly conceded by Ayden Heaven, who endured a particularly difficult game, as he lunged in recklessly, forcing Evanilson to jump out of the way or risk injury.

Justin Kluivert whipped the ball in beyond the far post and it was met by Rayan, who volleyed in low and precise. The Brazilian was unmarked. Carrick protested – at what? – and the Bournemouth supporters sang “you’re getting sacked in the morning”.

What a finish from Rayan to give Bournemouth the lead! 🔥 https://t.co/9BV0G5Tqgi

The outstanding Rayan should have had a hat-trick but failed to take two chances in the second half, when he only had goalkeeper Senne Lammens to beat, after Bournemouth had already doubled their lead. It came as Leny Yoro slipped over and presented the ball straight to Adrien Truffert, who squared it for Marcus Tavernier to side-foot home. It was that ridiculously easy.

The third was the same, with Evanilson chasing down a ball forward by Tyler Adams. The striker should not have got there. But Harry Maguire, captain in Fernandes’s absence, gave up, pointing at Lammens to win it. Instead, the goalkeeper was beaten to the ball and Evanilson’s finish from an angle, arcing high into the net, was superb.

"What a finish!" 😮‍💨 Evanilson makes it 3-0 to Bournemouth with a stunning goal https://t.co/hPMR78Z3cX

“You’re going down with the City,” goaded the Bournemouth fans and it is that end of the table United need to fret about. Which means, for Carrick, it has to be over. The Stretford End sang his name. But it was out of support for him as a player, his reputation, what he represented, not what is happening now as they once again vented their anger at the owners, director of football, Jason Wilcox, and even the plans for a new stadium.

It was the same as Carrick walked down the tunnel, thumping his chest as his name was sung. Then it turned. The vitriol, frustration and anger dripped down on the players, washing them away.

This felt like a new nadir. And the need for yet another new start away to Chelsea on Saturday.

Former Tottenham defender speaking to the BBC:

Manchester United’s players were just standing there today. I did not see in their body language that they are prepared to do everything for the manager, the club or the fans to change their situation.

It’s an easy thing to say they are lacking leaders but it’s true. They just don’t have big characters. It is not something technical but if you are in a tunnel and you saw the likes of [former Man Utd defenders] Nemanja Vidic or Rio Ferdinand their body language told the opposition that they were going to have a tough afternoon.

Carrick admits he does not know if he will remain in place.

The club have a week off now, with the next match a trip to Stamford Bridge against a tasty Chelsea side, albeit one who lost to Spurs last night.

He says: “It’s a tough situation. What is next? I don’t know. I’ll always do what’s best for this football club. I don’t change that now. I love what I do. I love the responsibility. But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Carrick gives a non-answer over his choice to leave Fernandes on the bench.

He says: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference but those are the decisions we made today.”

Carrick then denies that his acknowledgement of the crowd was to say goodbye, adding: “It wasn’t a farewell from me. I’m mixed emotions, I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell.

“Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.”

Carrick also tells Sky: “It’s really difficult to have a day like this at this football club and feel the emotion and dynamics of what it was like today.

“Not for me personally but for Manchester United. It was really mixed. I feel responsibility with the position I’m in. I’ve been at the club a long time. It hurts a lot going through this.”

Carrick potentially acknowledges that his time is up, telling Sky: “It was a strange, mixed of emotions at the end of the game. It wasn’t a nice way to end the game.

“It was a tough day for the players. We went into the game having been rocked. You can feel that. They’re really hurting and disappointed in there. It’s not a nice feeling. You have to accept it, we’re in that situation.”

Today’s United captain Harry Maguire tells Sky Sports: “It wasn’t good enough. Disappointed to give a goal away so early - another set play - and conceding first in the Premier League it makes it difficult.

“A mistake for the second makes it hard for ourselves. We didn’t perform well enough as individuals or as a team and we didn’t deserve anything from the game.

“It’s not clicking at the moment. Results are not good enough and performances in the last week not good enough. Still early in the season.

“Got to find something, question yourself, look in the mirror - that’s the most important thing - think what you can do more and what more you can contribute to the team and if we do that we’ll get somewhere.”

United players have said this for some time now. Each season they look in the mirror, and each season the supporters get the same.

Telegraph columnist Jamie Carragher thinks Carrick has had enough after that.

His emotional exit after the match suggested as much, with the former Liverpool player telling Sky: “He wants to be put out of his misery tonight.”

The fact that a mid-table team can come to Old Trafford and leave with three points is no longer a surprise.

If anything, it’s unusual when competent teams struggle against United these days.

Quite how replacing a manager changes a decade of falling short solves things, who knows?

At least the scoreline is not a surprise. Bournemouth always tend to win 3-0 at Old Trafford these days

Arne Slot underwhelmed last season, and Liverpool moved swiftly to appoint Andoni Iraola from Bournemouth.

They have defeated an impressive Brighton side 2-0 today, and you can read our report here.

Former Manchester United winger Ashley Young is scathing about the players who have succeeded him.

He told Sky Sports: “Unfortunately for Michael Carrick, it’s so disappointing. The fans are behind him and backing him and of course they are, because he’s a legend of the football club.

“But the players on the pitch showed nothing. They didn’t run, they didn’t look like a team together.

“If you looked at the difference to the Bournemouth team, you’d swap every single player for that Manchester United team. It was a poor showing.”

Extraordinary scenes at the end here. Carrick walks around the pitch waving at the fans and being applauded back. It felt very much like a manager saying goodbye. As he reached the Stretford End they start singing his song and Carrick responds by banging his chest in front of them. But as soon as the manager disappeared down the tunnel the fans instantly turned on the players trailing behind. A crescendo of sustained boos reverberate around as they target the players and make their feelings quite clear.

Picking Fernandes on the bench meant that Carrick got to snub him, but it also means that Sky get to make a point of his efforts to express himself, which does not really help the situation.

The away side now match Manchester City and Liverpool.

Now the pressure is on, the conversation has already moved onto what next.

Eddie Howe, Fabian Hurzeler, Antonio Conte, Julian Nagelsmann and Kieran McKenna are all in the frame to succeed Carrick if things go south soon.

What is striking is that none of the options are convincingly capable of such a vast, difficult task. That’s not their fault - it’s the owners’.

That’s the opinion of at least one managerial candidate linked with the United gig, should Carrick be given a healthy sum to walk away and take up an interest in koi carp.

With Fernandes dropped, that moment has probably got closer.

He writes: “A source close to one of United’s managerial candidates said: ‘It’s clear they need order and discipline. The dressing room is out of control and that is the first thing to fix.’

“That view was echoed by a friend of another candidate, who said: ‘The players talk too much. United is one of the biggest clubs in the world and that has to be respected.’”

Carrick had hinted as much in his pre-weekend press conference.

Fernandes’ zesty outburst, where he said United’s tactical failings against Como were “on the manager and staff” has understandably seen his position as United captain questioned.

Carrick did not rule it out, saying: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped for Manchester United’s crucial Premier League game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Michael Carrick has taken the decision to drop the United captain to the bench in the wake of his public criticism on Wednesday following the shambolic 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como.

Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics and has now been taken out of the starting XI.

The move had looked likely with Carrick refusing to rule out stripping Fernandes of the captaincy when quizzed on the matter on Friday.

Carrick had responded to Fernandes questioning the set up and approach by suggesting tactics can go out of the window when players are unprepared to run.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Manchester United vs Bouremouth.

United enter Sunday’s clash against Bournemouth in the grip of a deepening crisis. Wednesday night’s dismal 4-1 Champions League defeat to debutants Como extended United’s’ winless run to seven matches across all competitions - their worst sequence since 2015.

With just one victory from their opening seven Premier League fixtures, United are enduring their worst start to a top-flight season since 1986-87. Head coach Michael Carrick, a multiple champion at Old Trafford during his playing days, finds his position under severe threat, with reports suggesting another defeat could seal his departure. While both of United’s wins this season have come at home, they remain winless in their last three at Old Trafford. On an individual level, Bryan Mbeumo has offered a rare bright spark, scoring four goals in seven league outings while Bruno Fernandes continues to search for form, and the captain’s recent outburst only makes the atmosphere more febrile.

In stark contrast, Bournemouth arrive in Manchester brimming with confidence. Marco Rose’s side have enjoyed a flawless start to their inaugural European campaign, sitting joint-top of the Europa League standings after a dominant 3-0 victory over Ruben Amorim’s ten-man AC Milan on Thursday. That result marked a third consecutive home win and clean sheet, with Bournemouth outscoring opponents 8-0 in that stretch. Midfielder Marcus Tavernier has been instrumental, leading the club’s scoring charts with five goals across 11 appearances.

Bournemouth will feel no trepidation visiting Old Trafford, having gone unbeaten in their last six Premier League meetings with United (two wins, four draws). With Carrick desperate for a stabilising result and Rose’s side riding high on European momentum, today’s fixture carries significant stakes for both clubs.

#1178. A guide to the Nature Index

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The Nature Index is a database of author affiliations and institutional relationships. The index tracks contributions to research articles published in high-quality natural-science and health-science journals, chosen based on reputation by an independent group of researchers.

The Nature Index provides absolute and fractional counts of article publication at the institutional and national level and, as such, is an indicator of global high-quality research output and collaboration. Data in the Nature Index are updated regularly, with the most recent 12 months made available under a Creative Commons licence at natureindex.com. The database is compiled by Nature Portfolio.

The Nature Index uses Count and Share to track research output. A country/territory or an institution is given a Count of 1 for each article that has at least one author from that country/territory or institution. This is the case regardless of the number of authors an article has, and it means that the same article can contribute to the Count of multiple countries/territories or institutions.

To glean a country’s, territory’s, region’s or an institution’s contribution to an article, and to ensure that they are not counted more than once, the Nature Index uses Share, a fractional count that takes into account the share of authorship on each article. The total Share available per article is 1, which is shared among all authors under the assumption that each contributed equally. For instance, an article with 10 authors means that each author receives a Share of 0.1. For authors who are affiliated with more than one institution, the author’s Share is split equally between each institution. The total Share for an institution is calculated by summing the Share for individual affiliated authors. The process is similar for countries/territories, although complicated by the fact that some institutions have overseas labs that will be counted towards host country/territory totals.

Adjusted Share accounts for the annual variation in the total number of articles in the Nature Index journals. It is arrived at by calculating the percentage difference in the total number of articles in the Index in a given year relative to the number of articles in a base year and adjusting Share values to the base year levels.

The bilateral collaboration score (CS) between two institutions A+B is the sum of each of their Shares on the papers to which both have contributed. A bilateral collaboration can be between any two institutions or countries/territories co-authoring at least one article in the journals tracked by the Nature Index.

natureindex.com users can search for specific institutions or countries and generate their own reports, ordered by Count or Share.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03474-5

#1177. Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner

“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”

Kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and said: “You held it together. You got through it.” It showed how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

Kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

Kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

Bayern Munich and England's Ballon d'Or winner doing what he does best 🎯 https://t.co/yWNburqkpg

For his club, that is 19 goals more than any other player in the top five European leagues. And the most since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014-15. Kane won last season’s Golden Shoe by nine goals from Erling Haaland. He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Neither Kylian Mbappé nor Lamine Yamal, his closest rivals, scored in any finals.

Both gave interviews declaring why they should win the Ballon d’Or. Kane? “I don’t like talking about myself,” he said. “The 73 goals speak for themselves.” They do.

Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. Take his two goals against the Democratic Republic of Congo at the World Cup that saved his team and Thomas Tuchel from an embarrassing early exit.

The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

“A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments,” Prince William wrote on Instagram.

Kane, the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the award, is also the ultimate team player – so fulfilling that “collective performance” criteria – and a captain who leads by example on and off the pitch. Fair play? He was last booked in January and was cautioned just three times in 68 games and not at all in any of his 13 appearances this season.

And he works hard, so very hard. Kane was in the top 10 for total distance covered at the World Cup, despite playing a game fewer than most of the others on the list. And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

That work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and said he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

They probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

I can see why they don’t tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names there and there will be more people watching it if they don’t know so I can understand why.

From my point of view, of course I’d love to know to just kind of see and not have to wait throughout the whole night.

But it is their decision, I can’t control that. We’ll have to just enjoy it and try not to stress out too much.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

For the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more important than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

Kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

There's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN

Hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

First up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany said: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”

The plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has announced Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before quickly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

#1176. Revealed: The numbers that show Man United are NOT too good to go down - they have the worst defence in Europe, are constantly outrun by opponents and are one of the most wasteful teams in the Premier League

Published: 09:45 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 14:03 EST, 27 November 2026

Manchester United are not too good to go down and absolutely are in a relegation battle. They aren’t good, let’s start there.

Getting heavily beaten away to Liverpool was not at all surprising to Manchester United fans. If anything, many feared an even heavier scoreline.

Not since 1973-74 have Manchester United been relegated and on that occasion that rag-tag group had won three of its first 11 matches. This time around, the side Mauricio Pochettino has inherited has just one win to its name.

Former players and pundits believe that eventually, yes, United will get their act together and that relegation isn’t really something to be preoccupied with right now. Fools gold.

Chief executive Omar Berrada claimed with a straight face that the club is heading in the right direction only last week. As staggering a statement last Friday as it was by the time the final whistle sounded on Sunday. By that point, it was insulting.

Slumped in 19th and it will be 90 days since their last league win by the time they host Brentford at Old Trafford in a bid to stop the rot on Saturday, United’s problems are threatening to engulf Pochettino and his staff - even though they showed positive signs in the battling draw in Lisbon on Wednesday.

Daily Mail Sport takes a look at the stats that condemn this sorry United squad and why burying their heads in the hand at talk of a relegation battle is the last thing they can afford to do…

Manchester United are not too good to go down and absolutely are in a relegation battle

Trust Manchester United to be top of the table for the very worst statistic, officially having the worst defence in Europe’s top five leagues.

Luis Suarez's late goal for Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday made it 36 goals conceded in total by United across all competitions, taking them ahead of Lens (35), Crystal Palace (34), Getafe (34) and Union Berlin (33).

That’s a Lens side that conceded nine in one match in the Champions League. That’s an Union Berlin side who has conceded five or more goals three times already this campaign, including a 7-0 drubbing at the hands of Bayern Munich.

Individually and collectively United lack any sort of structure, any sort of desire to do the basics, any sort of solidity that will have opposition forwards thinking twice.

Open it up to the top four leagues in England and United are one of only two teams yet to manage a single league clean sheet this season, with fellow Premier League outfit Ipswich Town. League Two side Barnet was on that list until they kept their first clean sheet of the season against Crawley on Tuesday.

Specifically in the Premier League, United rank 19th for Big Chances Against (22.2), rank 19th for Expected Goals Against (xGA). They have the sixth-worst Expected Goals differential in the league.

The Red Devils have the worst defence in Europe’s top five leagues, conceding 36 goals so far

Matthijs de Ligt looked all at sea in his first league start in 357 days away to Liverpool to the point whereby Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher said they ‘felt sorry’ for him. Leny Yoro continues to make costly mistakes. Diogo Dalot no longer looks up to the level. Noussair Mazraoui has regressed massively. Patrick Dorgu looks uncomfortable defending. Harry Maguire lacks recovery pace to go toe-to-toe with top defenders. Ayden Heaven is raw. Lisandro Martinez is a shadow of the best version previously seen at United. And Luke Shaw is injured.

It a defence that is majorly short on quality, discipline and leadership and that’s underscored by the amount of times they concede in bunches.

United shipped two goals in eight minutes away to Como and conceded two in five minutes a few days later against Bournemouth.

Twice in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa they conceded in bunches with two first half goals in three minutes, followed up by two Villa goals in five minutes in the second.

Add in the two goals in six minutes at home against Roma – a game where the attack bailed out the defence in a 3-2 win – and the two goals shipped at Anfield in three minutes against Liverpool, this United rearguard is not fit for purpose.

Put these defenders in a neutral kit and unanimously they’d be seen as relegation candidates.

Mauricio Pochettino must sort out Manchester United's leaky defence as a top priority

That’s what set pieces are to United, a complete disaster.

Poor sides in the Premier League often must hang their hats on scoring timely goals and grinding out vital wins through the means of set-pieces.

United do not look capable of doing that.

In the Premier League, they are joint-20th for set-piece goals conceded so far this season with seven, while they rank 19th for set-piece goals scored (1). Only Nottingham Forest (0) are performing worse in this area than United.

Set-piece xG places United 19th in the league with 2.6, only marginally ahead of Gary O’Neil’s Ipswich Town, who are 20th with a set-piece xG of 1.6.

Hull City boss Sergej Jakirovic hinted after the opening weekend’s 2-0 win over United that the Red Devils are easy to prepare for when it comes to set pieces, the area which created both goals.

Last season United ranked second, only behind champions Arsenal, for set-piece goals scored and 11th for set-piece goals conceded.

Pochettino took issue with Chelsea’s hierarchy when they went over his head to appoint a dedicated set-piece coach and there is no suggestion one such guru is heading United’s way.

But make no bones about it, United have regressed massively in this area and it’s a slide without an easy fix.

Luis Suarez capitalises on Senne Lammens' error to equalise for Sporting Lisbon late on

One of the biggest concerns right now is the ease at which teams are cutting United open.

Bournemouth are a very good team but their win at Old Trafford looked like a training game at times.

Against Villa, John McGinn strolled through the game, even if they went on to draw 4-4. There are too many examples of this.

At 111.5km on average per game, United rank 19th in the league for distance covered per match, with only Sunday’s victors Liverpool clocking in further ground coverage.

Worse than that, United badly lack pace and athleticism in the middle of the park as well as in wide areas. Where Liverpool fans marvel at the likes of Rio Ngumoha and Bradley Barcola, United have built a squad severely lacking pace in all areas.

Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha are better inside and lack blistering pace. Diogo Dalot and Luke Shaw have both been exposed defensively for pace this season. Kobbie Mainoo and Youri Tielemans are technically very good operators but both lack athleticism and are therefore losing the midfield battle too often.

Pochettino’s predecessor Michael Carrick scoffed at the fixation on running stats before he was sacked and there is some merit to it not being the be-all-and-end-all – look at Liverpool.

But only Aston Villa (10) have been outrun by opponents more through the opening 11 games than United (9) and that, factored in with a porous defence and a soft underbelly at set pieces has United out there like a lamb for slaughter a lot of the time.

The appointment of Sam Wilson as first-team fitness coach, a move agreed long in advance of Pochettino’s hiring, from Arsenal will look to address the serious levels of underperformance in this area.

But with so little time on the training pitch and free moments in the schedule to fix months of fitness regression, it’s a gargantuan task.

Man United badly lack pace and athleticism in the middle of the park as well as in wide areas

As Pochettino had his head in his hands at Anfield he’d have been forgiven for wondering just how he was actually going to stop this sinking ship from fully going under.

He was back at Carrington at 6:30am on Monday morning staring at a schedule that promises 10 games in 39 days.

Players were back in for recovery sessions on Monday and training on Tuesday ahead of flying to Lisbon to face Sporting on Wednesday. Despite picking up a first point under Pochettino, there were plenty of individual errors in the 2-2 draw, namely with Senne Lammens conceding a needless penalty and later gifting Sporting an equaliser after failing to gather the ball in the air.

With recovery on Thursday, it means there is only time for a light Friday session pre-Brentford on Saturday, when it will have been 90 days since United’s last league win.

For all of the reasons outlined above, United are like a boxer on the ropes that is just trying to hang in there for the remainder of the year as the blows keep raining down.

There are problems aplenty in defence and athleticism is one of the biggest worries. But mentality and belief is what Pochettino and his staff need to inspire as soon as possible.

With a busy schedule of games, Pochettino and his coaching team don't have time on their side

United are the only team in the Premier League not to win a single game across the last seven, while they are one of only two teams in the 92 in the Football League to have just one domestic win this season, along with Burnley.

Having fallen behind eight times in the league, United have gone on to win just once, beating Ipswich Town. That was the anomaly.

From winning positions, they rank 19th for points won, taking just six points from the four games in which they held the lead.

And, ultimately, what are United’s players and fans clinging to?

They rank 17th for home form and 19th away from home, where they have scored just four goals, while they are 18th in the league for shot conversion (5%) having taken the most shots (280) in the league. Only Sunderland and Nottingham Forest are more wasteful.

United still have to travel to Newcastle United and Arsenal before the year is out, both daunting trips for sides low on confidence, while Champions League hopes hang in the balance against Sporting and RB Leipzig.

Pochettino has a list as long as his arm with what he needs to fix but he has to get players believing again. It’s November and things are bad now, but they cannot throw in the towel when the going gets tough.

At this stage, indications are that the budget to be afforded to Pochettino in January will be ‘modest’ and is not set to be the splurge United likely need it to be.

Calvin Bassey and Nathan Collins are on a list of targets, while Jarrad Branthwaite has been admired for a long time, albeit would be a player who would prove very expensive to get out of Everton mid-season.

United need to add at least two high-quality defenders in January, if not three, to give them a chance of salvaging a season that is threatening to get away from them.

The likes of Maguire, De Ligt, Dalot and Mazraoui are not suddenly going to improve and while there is a belief among former players that they won’t go down and it’s not a conversation to be had, those upstairs, who have failed miserably to date, cannot afford to show the same level of flippancy in what is set to be the most critical transfer window in decades for United.

Get it wrong and they could run out of road come May.

Indications are that the budget to be afforded to Pochettino by Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left) and Omar Berrada (right) in January will be ‘modest’, despite Manchester United needing reinforcements

It raised alarm last Sunday night when it was pointed out that Tottenham Hotspur, who finished 17th and survived by the skin of their teeth last season, had 18 points after 11 games last season, 10 points more than United currently have.

In fact, since 2019-20, 20 different teams have had eight or fewer points after 11 Premier League games and 14 have gone down.

Two seasons ago both Crystal Palace and Wolverhampton Wanderers sat with fewer points than United after 11 games and both survived comfortably.

But the general trend is those there now will be there when all is said and done.

#1175. Supreme Court makes CVC vote annulment final, but LaLiga’s December deal approval stands

Spain's Supreme Court has refused LaLiga's appeal, making final the annulment of the August 2021 assembly vote on the CVC deal, a case won by Real Madrid and Athletic Club. It is a legal win for the two clubs, but the later December 2021 approval behind LALIGA Impulso remains in force.

Spain’s Supreme Court has thrown out LaLiga’s cassation appeal against the Madrid Provincial Court judgment on the CVC operation. The General Assembly resolution of 12 August 2021, which approved the deal, therefore stays void for good. Real Madrid and Athletic Club brought the winning case. LaLiga now carries the costs of the failed appeal.

The decision closes a five-year legal fight over that single vote. In August 2021, Barcelona, Athletic Club and Real Madrid jointly announced a challenge to the resolution. They argued it broke Royal Decree-Law 5/2015 and was passed through a highly irregular process.

Real Madrid described the annulled resolution as one of huge economic significance. In the club’s account, it was passed before clubs had enough information to judge the scope, impact and consequences of changes to the operation. The club also highlighted the court’s remark that LaLiga’s appeal tried to replace the Provincial Court’s view with LaLiga’s own self-interested view.

LaLiga reads the decision more narrowly. The annulled assembly approved the term sheet of the CVC project, and the appeal fell for lack of cassation interest. LaLiga said the court issued a procedural order rather than a judgment endorsing the Provincial Court’s reasoning, and did not examine the substance of the case.

The deal itself does not depend on the annulled vote. LaLiga’s General Assembly approved the LALIGA Impulso project later, on 10 December 2021. Under the deal, clubs received around €2bn in exchange for a share of the value of the competition’s audiovisual rights over 50 years. A new company set up by LaLiga and the fund manages that arrangement. Real Madrid, Barcelona and Athletic Club rejected it and stayed out.

Those December resolutions have survived their own court test. In June 2026, Section 18 of the Madrid Provincial Court rejected in full the appeal by Athletic Club and Real Madrid against them. It upheld the first-instance judgment of 19 February 2024 and ordered both clubs to pay the costs of that hearing. The court found that clubs still own their audiovisual rights, while LaLiga sells them collectively under the law. It also ruled that creating LaLiga Group International, owned jointly by LaLiga and CVC, did not breach the Sports Law or LaLiga’s statutes.

That leaves the practical picture largely unchanged. Iusport, a Spanish sports-law outlet, described the Supreme Court order as having no practical effect on the LaLiga–CVC deal. The ruling still matters for how LaLiga is run, because it confirms that one of its assembly votes on the operation was unlawful. The league insists it respects court decisions and will keep defending the agreements backed by most of its clubs.

The fight over the December agreements is not over either. Real Madrid has taken that ruling to the Supreme Court, which has not yet decided whether to admit the appeal.

#1174. Hull City drop Roma loanee Robinio Vaz after Paris police incident

Roma loanee Robinio Vaz has been left out of Hull City’s squad for Sunday’s Premier League game against Crystal Palace after an incident in Paris this week.

According to talkSPORT, the 19-year-old forward was reportedly detained by French police on suspicion of fraud involving a hire car. The car had been flagged as stolen because its owner had missed lease payments. Vaz was released without charge after the matter was dropped. However, Hull say they did not know he had travelled to France.

Hull coach Sergej Jakirović told the BBC he only found out when Robinio Vaz failed to turn up for training on Tuesday.

“It’s not good behaviour, I can say like this. It’s not professional,” he said. “I know he is young, but you are a professional player, you need to be very, very careful especially in private life.”

Jakirović confirmed Hull are now in talks with Roma to find a solution. “He is not our player, he is on loan here, so it’s a Roma decision,” he added.

Roma signed Vaz from Marseille in January for a fee reported at around €25m. He then joined Hull on a season-long loan with an option to buy on deadline day. Things have not gone to plan in England, though. He has made only five substitute appearances, totalling around 50 minutes, and has been unable to dislodge Oli McBurnie.

#1173. Ten-man Tenerife beat Badajoz 5-2 in Copa del Rey tie postponed after De Miguel’s death

Tenerife won 5-2 at Badajoz in the Copa del Rey despite finishing the match with ten men. The victory keeps their cup run alive ahead of the second-round draw.

At the Estadio Nuevo Vivero on Wednesday 18 November, Álvaro Cervera’s side booked a place in the second round of the Copa del Rey. The tie had been postponed twice, first after the train accident in Toledo province and then after the death of Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel on 3 November, who was remembered with a minute’s silence.

Cervera started a line-up made up largely of reserves. It still produced a scoreline Tenerife had never recorded in 260 Copa del Rey matches, according to elDiario.es (Canarias Ahora). About 3,000 spectators watched, around 20 per cent of the stadium’s capacity.

Grant-Leon Ranos opened the scoring in the sixth minute from a Marc Mateu assist. Juanjo Sánchez added a second a minute later. Ranos struck again in the 38th minute, set up by Gerard Valentín.

Carlos Beitia pulled one back for Badajoz in the 49th minute. Roko Jureškin was then sent off in the 58th minute. Ten-man Tenerife still extended the lead through substitute Iván Chapela in the 69th minute, assisted by Martin Pečar.

Jorge Barba replied for the hosts in the 74th minute from a Manuel Hernández assist. Víctor Moreno completed the scoring deep into stoppage time, with Álvarez providing the pass.

The Segunda Federación side went into the tie third in their group. They were also unbeaten in seven league matches in a row.

Tenerife have now come through their opening Copa del Rey tie in eight seasons in a row. The win followed a 2-0 victory over AD Ceuta FC. Before that came a run of draws against FC Andorra, Sabadell, Celta de Vigo II and Girona.

This was the first meeting between the clubs in the cup. They had played each other 22 times in Segunda División. Tenerife won ten of those games, Badajoz eight, and four ended level. Tenerife’s previous visit to Badajoz, on 30 March 2003, ended in a 2-1 defeat under David Amaral.

#1172. Fleetwood knock out Arsenal in one of biggest shocks in League Cup history

Leaving Highbury was a wrench for Arsenal in 2006, but it was not the case 20 years later. They could not wait to get out of the stadium with the same name after a night that left Mikel Arteta looking haunted.

Fleetwood Town did not have any marble halls; they did not even have enough space in their car park for the three coaches carrying Arsenal’s entourage, but they have a proud tradition, spirit and, as a result, they will dine out on a result that will be celebrated for months and talked about for decades.

Eighty-four rungs separated these teams at kick-off, but, now and again, you get a situation when the floodlights are on, belief is high and the sense of history is prevalent. It is an intoxicating combination and, gloriously, the stars aligned. Mission impossible was completed.

Having chiselled out a 1-1 draw in 90 minutes in which Max Dowman was sent off, Fleetwood dispatched five nerveless spot-kicks, the last one thundered in by Conor Haughey after Bruno Guimarães’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch.

“You have got to have confidence, haven’t you?” Haughey asked. “I just thought, I’m going to run up and smack it. It’s incredible. I come from Belfast and if you don’t have confidence, you will get eaten up.”

This was ignominious for Arsenal, an elimination from this tournament to rival the 1969 loss in the final to Swindon Town or the 2012 exit to Bradford, then also of League Two. What made this so astonishing was the fact that Mikel Arteta went so strong.

You should never be surprised by anything these days, but, even still, an eight-minute delay because of a drone flying over this wonderful little venue would not have been on anyone’s bingo card. Only 57 seconds had been played when Michael Salisbury, the referee, saw a light in the sky and said “stop”.

A drone stops play at the Highbury Stadium. https://t.co/TvjNjjACFM

The precaution was understandable. Only 10 days ago, one idiot escaped from a village to kick a rugby ball off the roof of an apartment block into the Gtech Community Stadium while Brentford and Liverpool were playing and could have caused serious injury.

So while the locals harrumphed as the players tried to keep themselves warm, no risk could be taken. Eventually, police apprehended the operator in a nearby park. It was something unfathomable, which was also true of what happened when the contest resumed.

The anticipation was that Arsenal would saunter clear against opponents who had lost at Exeter City on Saturday, leaving them 18th in England’s fourth tier. But it only took a few skirmishes to appreciate this was not going to be the cakewalk anticipated in what was the biggest occasion in Fleetwood’s history.

Arteta absolutely knew his team were not operating at the levels they should have been. He was wrapped up against the elements in a thick black jacket but, every so often, he would express his exasperation at Jurriën Timber, captain for the night, to “get forward!”

They were in a battle, that much was obvious, and one challenge from Shaun Rooney – so forceful you thought the ball might burst – sent Myles Lewis-Skelly spinning like a top. How Fleetwood’s fans loved it, roaring their approval as the young England international hit the ground with a thump.

Arsenal had one good chance when Dowman skipped down the right and dragged a shot across the box that Viktor Gyökeres could not divert but then, wonderfully, things took a totally unexpected turn when Fleetwood poked their noses in front.

It was a League Two goal in its simplicity, but that is no criticism. Harrison Neal helped a long ball forward, putting it behind Marli Salmon and Aaron Loupalo-Bi relished the chance to get into a foot race, grappling with the England Under-17 international.

Salmon looked like he had him at one point, but Loupalo-Bi was strong – not to mention composed – and he held off the challenge to slide a left-footed shot through the legs of Illan Meslier, who was making his Arsenal debut. What followed was unique to the magic of an English cup tie.

FLEETWOOD TAKE THE LEAD! 😱 Loupalo-Bi puts League Two side Fleetwood ahead against Arsenal 💥 https://t.co/zTFEkCp0oL

As the home fans set off flares, filling the air with plumes of thick, red smoke, the theme tune to Captain Pugwash was played. Arteta tried to find answers from his coaching staff, amid the cacophony, but occasionally you do not have to look too deep for answers.

Could the miracle happen? When half-time arrived with Fleetwood still in the lead, you began to wonder. But then you saw Ben White and Martin Odegaard go through intense warm-ups so they could be introduced at the start of the second half and you knew the mountain had become taller.

So it proved. Odegaard, with his mesmerising left foot and all-encompassing vision, did more in the first five minutes of the second period than many of his colleagues had managed before the interval, and Arsenal levelled in that initial flurry through Gyökeres’s first domestic goal of the campaign.

Viktor Gyökeres gets his first goal of the season and Arsenal are level against Fleetwood! 🔴 https://t.co/LfZcIbAfCX

A game of attack against defence played out for the remainder before Dowman was harshly dismissed in the 85th minute after reacting to a tough challenge from Neal. There was still time for Fleetwood’s Lynch to make two excellent saves from White and Odegaard in added time as Arsenal tried to avoid the shoot-out lottery. They could not and how it hurt them.

HUGE save from Jay Lynch! https://t.co/dLJaFwCmHQ

“Football’s getting a little bit more, I don’t know, clinical and removed,” Matt Lawlor, the Fleetwood manager, said. “To me, there was that feeling we all get as football fans. That was what you kind of live for, isn’t it? To be a part of it is special.

“To be giving that to football fans and especially Fleetwood fans is unbelievably special. I’m really proud of it. Football’s a funny old game, isn’t it?”

First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through in the next round, in the manner they’ve done it, the atmosphere they have created, and, yeah, a really sad day for us.

I cannot fault at all the attitude of the players. I haven’t seen anyone not doing what is required at this level. But, obviously, we insisted so much, we have so much of the ball, so many chances, so many shots, and if you want the margins to be bigger than going to the penalties, obviously, you need to capitalise on that. And we didn’t. And football is about that.

Attitude wise, absolutely zero [wrong] otherwise, I would be here absolutely fuming. I’m sad, I think we are all sad. We have a massive responsibility to carry this badge in the best possible way. It had nothing to do with effort or application or determination to win it, but we lack other things to, to create a much bigger margin than today, with what we produce, they really should have been shown in the scoreline.

Something that we discussed already before the match.

It’s difficult to see on the cameras, I prefer to watch it back properly and I will assess the situation.

Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz and Eberechi Eze are among the players stepping off the bus, so at the very least it will be a strong bench.

Aside from their stadium being called Highbury, Fleetwood Town’s red shirts with white sleeves also bear a striking resemblance to Arsenal’s home kit. The club in its current guise was founded in 1997, although previous iterations date back to 1908 under the name Fleetwood FC.

There is no evidence or anecdote suggesting Arsenal were the inspiration, so it appears the kit clash is a coincidence. Arsenal will be wearing their navy away strip.

The club’s most famous son is surely Jamie Vardy, who scored 31 goals in 36 appearances for Fleetwood in the 2011-12 season before Leicester City made their move.

An unfamiliar opponent at a very familiar sounding venue, Arsenal play Fleetwood Town for the first time this evening at the Lancashire club’s Highbury Stadium.

Fleetwood, 18th in League Two, are the lowest-ranked team remaining in this season’s League Cup, having booked their place in the fourth round thanks to a victory at Sheffield United.

They were playing in English football’s sixth tier in 2009, and so while their stadium may share its name with Arsenal’s former home, the two clubs are worlds apart.

The League Cup is fourth of four competitions on Arsenal’s list of priorities, but Mikel Arteta should be able to rotate extensively while progressing to the quarter-finals. With a trip to Anfield on Sunday, that is a welcome luxury.

Kepa Arrizabalaga, Piero Hincapie, Cristhian Mosquera, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyokeres are seasoned internationals in need of minutes and in line to start.

Max Dowman lit up Arsenal’s third-round victory at Ipswich Town, and 17-year-old centre-back Marli Salmon was not far behind him. Young striker and Northern Ireland international Ceadach O’Neill is also expected to be involved, and he may be joined by other academy players.

While attention is fixed on Premier League and Champions League success, Arsenal’s stinging defeat by Manchester City in last season’s final of this competition will not have been forgotten by Arteta or his players.

Matt Lawlor, Fleetwood’s manager, was full of praise for Arsenal in his pre-match press conference: “The champions are coming to town and they’re coming to our patch. The players need to be excited by it, not overawed by it. The respect is through the roof, but the fear can’t be through the roof.

“We’ve earned a game like this. We’ve had to go through round upon round of tough games, and none of them were easy. To get to where we are, we deserve that.”

Arteta has told his players that they must keep their standards high, with a lack of concentration or professionalism potentially their worst enemy against fourth-tier opposition.

Arteta said: “Our reputation, our pride, everything is in play. So every time you play a football match, and especially against a team in a different division, respect the game, respect every opponent because they deserve that, and then try to win and try to play a bit better than them.“We know the risk, and in football, things can get very equal the moment you are able to match certain things, and that’s why our basics and habits have to be through the roof to be able to win the game.”Full team news on the way shortly.

#1171. Ronaldo reveals why he left Barcelona for Inter in 1997

Ronaldo has revealed that money was the main reason he left Barcelona for Inter in 1997, with the Nerazzurri offering him four times his salary at the Camp Nou.

The Brazilian legend was speaking on the Stick to Football podcast with Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher, in a special episode released today on Disney+.

Ronaldo spent just one season at Barcelona after joining from PSV, but it was a spectacular one. He scored goal after goal in La Liga and the Cup Winners’ Cup before Inter paid his release clause to bring him to Serie A.

“Barça bought me for 20 million, and I received a good chunk of that. There, I was earning two million a year, and Inter offered me eight, so I decided to go,” he explained.

Ronaldo said he was still angry about the 1996 Ballon d’Or, when he was voted in second place behind Matthias Sammer.

“I lost it to Sammer, who was a defender. I was angry because I’d played fantastically with Barcelona and scored so many goals,” he said.

He made up for it in his first season in Milan, winning the Ballon d’Or in 1997 as an Inter player. He won it again in 2002.

Il Fenomeno also suggested modern forwards don’t know how lucky they are.

“Today’s strikers have an easier life than we did. I’d have liked to have the same protection. We suffered so much. Our generation was full of killers, and nobody protected us,” he said with a laugh.

Ronaldo was less upbeat about the Brazil national team. He admitted Argentina’s fighting spirit is “painful” to watch for Brazilians.

“I think we’re copying European players. Before, there was always very high confidence in our country based purely on our talent. But Europeans today are stronger, faster, more organised, and play better,” he said. “Brazil aren’t strong enough to win the World Cup. We don’t have a strong team, we’re not united.”

#1170. KASPER HOGH - THE £11M ENIGMA: Until such time as Celtic can cut their losses on the misfit striker, Martin O'Neill has a problem on his hands

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 14:08 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 14:14 EST, 27 November 2026

On the website of Pluto Data Analytics, prospective clients are given a taste of what they can expect if they form a partnership with the London-based company.

Under a section headed ‘Transferability You Can Trust,’ football clubs are told: ‘At Pluto, we use advanced machine learning to validate how a player might adapt in a new league.

‘For example, how would a defender in Japan’s J1 League perform in the MLS in America? This kind of insight supports clubs to make smarter, more confident recruitment decisions across borders.’

We’ll never know, of course, how different Celtic’s summer transfer dealings might have been had they got into bed with the company before this week.

But on one question, in particular, the Parkhead club would have been likely to have seen more red flags raised than a communist parade.

‘How would a forward who’s so clearly tailor-made for a unique environment north of the Arctic circle fare in the Scottish Premiership?’ Well, not too great, as it turns out.

Hogh endured another tough night in Portugal as his goalless run extended to 17 games

Listen, you didn’t need to have a PhD in mathematics to question the wisdom of Celtic paying a record £11million to sign Kasper Hogh from Bodo/Glimt in the summer. Just an appreciation that so many players who’ve thrived at that extraordinary club have found success hard to come by elsewhere.

This observation is hardly new. It’s been the subject of discussions throughout Europe since the impressive Kjetil Knutsen began establishing a culture at the Norwegian outpost in 2018, one which would pave the way to four titles, a cup and a run to the semi-finals of the Europa League.

Knutsen and his sizeable entourage have created a world of their own 520 miles north of Oslo. And the dogs in the street know that those who venture outside it rarely do well.

Sure, Victor Boniface, now of Bayer Leverkusen, hasn’t really looked back since leaving for Union Saint-Gilloise. And Hugo Vetlesen has done well since moving to Club Brugge two years ago.

But they are outnumbered by those who looked lost the minute Bodo/Glimt sold them. Patrick Berg, Fredrik Bjorkan and Jens Petter Hauge, to name but three.

Were Celtic not aware of this curious trend as Bodo/Glimt somehow convinced them to part with a club-record fee? Or did their research only go as far as the five goals Hogh scored in the Champions League last season?

Provided this Tuesday’s annual general meeting does not descend into disarray, an explanation from someone involved in the deal would be fitting.

Hogh wasn’t some six-figure punt, after all. He was an eight-figure sure thing. Or, at least, that’s what the Celtic hierarchy believed him to be.

Who first flagged him up and who agreed that he was worthy of such a gargantuan investment? The trouble with Celtic these days is that no one is quite sure about who’s responsible for that kind of thing.

Despite Paul Tisdale leaving his head of football operations post on January 5, the club has yet to appoint a replacement. Nor has the vacant role been reclassified to that of director of football or sporting director.

Two months previously, chief scout Jay Lefevre left for Swansea. Despite Mark Cooper effectively filling that void and former Chelsea operative James Bell-Walker joining the team in January, officially, there is still no head of recruitment.

O'Neill turned to Columbian hitman Duran to get Celtic out of a hole against Torreense

That’s just not a good look when the collective decision in June was to go all-in on a player who’s now gone 17 games without a goal.

Celtic’s partnership with the analytics company is all well and good and may indeed sharpen up the club’s future recruitment. It certainly needs it.

But it can’t undo what’s already done. And until such time as the club can cut its losses on Hogh and sign a replacement, Martin O’Neill has a serious problem on his hands.

Starting at Tynecastle tomorrow and up to the visit to Ibrox on January 3, Celtic have eight games to play.

That run includes a trip to Cyprus to face Omonia Nicosia, which now carries added significance after Thursday’s narrow win over Torreense revived the club’s Europa League hopes.

The trouble is that Hogh can no longer be trusted to deliver in any of those crucial matches. That much became abundantly clear across his dismal 59-minute contribution in Portugal.

That old cliché about strikers always being judged on goals has never actually rang true. Provided they hold the ball up and facilitate their team-mates to score, there will always be a degree of forgiveness.

Hogh’s epic goalless run stretching back to the hat-trick he hit at Kilmarnock on August 9 is only one part of the story now. It’s his inability to do the fundamentals of football — securing possession and finding a man — which have taken him to the point of no return.

This is no longer about one man needing a scruffy goal to get going. That’s just not going to happen. He’s demonstrably the wrong fit for Celtic. He has been a scandalous waste of money.

His display against Torreense was that of a player who is getting worse by the week, not better. He touched the ball just 13 times, misplaced three passes and only found a team-mate on seven occasions.

Hogh’s one moment of promise came when he robbed veteran defender Stopira in the right channel just before half-time. Having done the hard part and got to the line, his cut-back went straight into the goalkeeper’s arms.

Hogh's confidence already looks shot after making a miserable start to his Celtic career

‘It’s poor. It’s really poor. He is really lacking conviction,’ said former Celtic manager Neil Lennon.

Hogh’s withdrawal came not a moment too soon for the visiting fans. With approximately half as much time on the pitch, his replacement, Camilo Duran, managed just one touch fewer than the Dane, including the header for the winning goal which came from James Forrest’s cross.

Now with 15 goals for the season after signing from Qarabag for an initial £4.5m, the Colombian is continuing to prove that spending money is one thing. It’s how you spend it which is crucial.

O’Neill is hardly without options across the front area as a defining spell begins in Gorgie.

After being sidelined for 18 months with a serious knee injury, Jota’s display against Torreense was scintillating. There should be no concerns now over the £8m which was spent to bring him back to the club.

While Yang Hyun-jun had a poor night in Portugal, it was a rarity in recent times. The Korean is a different animal to the one which arrived from Gangwon FC three years back for £2.2m.

Haissem Hassan, Yang’s main rival on the right, hasn’t kicked a ball in Celtic’s last three matches. The fact that Forrest and Seb Tounekti stepped off the bench on Thursday before the £6m Egyptian was instructive.

Intriguingly, Callum Osmand remained there throughout. It won’t have escaped anyone’s notice that the 20-year-old arrived from Fulham ostensibly as a centre-forward.

He was recently afforded opportunities on the wing as Jota got back up to speed, but with the Portuguese returning to top form, that door is closing.

Osmand shouldn’t lose much sleep over that recent development, though. Without even shedding his tracksuit in Leiria, he jumped ahead of the hapless Hogh in the pecking order.

#1169. Real Madrid tie Tchouaméni and Güler to 2032 contracts within 24 hours

Real Madrid have extended the contracts of Aurélien Tchouaméni and Arda Güler until June 2032, a day apart. With captain Fede Valverde also reportedly agreeing new terms, the club are securing their core midfield for years to come.

Real Madrid have committed two midfield regulars to long-term deals in the space of 24 hours. Güler’s announcement came first, and Aurélien Tchouaméni’s followed.

Both players are part of the core of Mourinho’s midfield. The renewals keep them at the club for six more seasons.

Tchouaméni arrived in 2022 and has made 205 appearances for the club. He has won eight trophies in that time. They include one Champions League, two Club World Cups and two UEFA Super Cups. He has also lifted one LaLiga, one Copa del Rey and one Spanish Super Cup.

His standing goes beyond the club. He has 50 France caps and won the 2021 Nations League. The new contract is worth around €9 million net per season, GOAL reported. The agreement came after interest from Manchester United.

Güler’s record covers a shorter spell. He was 18 when he joined. He has 38 caps for Turkey. In September he was named Breakthrough Player of the 2025-26 Champions League. His new salary is reportedly about €8m a year.

The two profiles differ. Tchouaméni is an established international with a full set of club honours. Güler is a younger player whose contract now runs almost nine years from his arrival. Tying both to the same end date suggests a midfield the club intend to keep together.

The club may not be finished. Captain Fede Valverde has agreed to extend his contract from 2029 to 2031, according to GOAL. The new deal will make him one of the squad’s highest earners. An announcement is expected soon, as Madrid work on further renewals after Güler and Tchouaméni.

If Valverde’s extension is confirmed, none of the three midfielders would have a contract ending before 2031. That would remove contract questions over a key part of the squad for several seasons. The two completed renewals arrived during the build-up to a busy run of home matches.

🚨🤍 Aurelien Tchouameni has signed new long term deal at Real Madrid until June 2032. pic.twitter.com/13BtcLyubP

— Fabrizio Romano (@FabrizioRomano) November 19, 2026

Tchouaméni has not been fully clear of fitness concerns this month. Earlier in November he left the France squad with a muscle problem. He was back in training with the Madrid squad on the day his renewal was announced.

Real Madrid host Celta at the Santiago Bernabéu on Saturday 21 November at 21:00 in LaLiga matchday 13. PSV then visit for a Champions League game on Tuesday 24 November.
